#1541. Luke Graham seizes his chance to shine in Scotland back-line... now Stoke defender aims to make himself a fixture for years to come

By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER

Published: 17:30 EST, 14 November 2026 | Updated: 18:01 EST, 14 November 2026

Whatever concerns there may legitimately be about the limited progress seen in Sebastien Pocognoli’s brief time in charge of Scotland, the Belgian has hardly been blessed with good fortune.

In five matches to date in the Nations League, the manager has not yet been able to select the same back-three in two consecutive outings. Injuries and suspensions have seen to that.

For all that, you sense that even if he’d had a full quota of players to choose from, Pocognoli would still be figuring out his preferred defensive grouping.

This does feel like a time of opportunity for those who are fresh on the scene. Catch the eye and there’s a real chance to become established as a mainstay of the team moving forward.

Luke Graham did his chances of doing just that no harm at all in his first start and second cap for his country on Friday.

Playing in between Ryan Porteous and Kieran Tierney, the Stoke City man made a compelling case to stay there with a strong and diligent display.

Luke Graham enjoyed a composed debut for Scotland as they recorded a much-needed win

On the back of a summer move from Dundee to the English Championship, Graham appears to have taken the step-up to international level in his stride.

‘It’s something I’ve always wanted to do since I was growing up, so I have to be ready for the moment and take it when it comes,’ he said.

‘I think there’s good competition. We have a lot of good centre-halves. Obviously, it was unfortunate for Welshy (Stephen Welsh) and Binksy (Luis Binks) to go out with injury, but that opens up a space for me to come in and try to cement a place.

‘When you’re out on that pitch, you have to do everything you can to try and stay in the team. I gave my all and I’ll just need to wait and see what happens going forward.’

Timing can be vital in football. And it’s conceivable that Graham’s might just propel him to become a Scotland regular.

While playing at Dens Park saw him mentioned in dispatches with regards to a call-up, his move to England, coming just before Pocognoli was announced as Steve Clarke’s successor, has seen his dream quickly become reality.

‘I’ve always said that one thing I wanted to do in my career was play for Scotland, so to get it over the line was pretty special,’ he reflected.

Former Dundee defender Graham proudly belts out the national anthem ahead of kick-off

‘Not much is going wrong for me at the moment, so it’s just about maintaining that and keeping it going every week.

‘I wouldn’t say I merited a start as we have a lot of good players in the camp. It’s up to the manager to pick the team and, luckily, he gave me the chance.

‘He just said to go out and enjoy it and do what you’re doing every week at Stoke. I think I did all right.’

Notwithstanding how limited the North Macedonians were on the night, Pocognoli was entitled to take encouragement from the way the back three acquitted themselves.

Playing closer to each other than we’d seen in the previous matches, they were rarely unpicked by balls through the middle. Angus Gunn was not overworked in goal. Tellingly, the only concession of the night came when Scott McTominay lost his man at a corner.

‘I think a lot of it is just being brave,’ Graham reflected. ‘It’s about bravery in going man-to-man with the striker, being brave on the ball, trying to break the lines and keeping possession.

‘So, I think bravery is the main thing and concentration as well.’

Graham keeps a close eye on North Macedonian danger man Elmin Rastoder at Hampden

With the defence solid enough, Pocognoli had a platform for a much-needed win. While the narrow scoreline made the final moments more anxious than they should have been, on balance, Scotland were deserved winners.

‘It’s just about winning games at this stage of the competition, so that was good,’ said Graham. ‘I think, if I’m being harsh, we should have killed the game off before it got to 1-1. We had a few good chances to put them to bed.

‘Then we kinda shot ourselves in the foot by conceding from a set piece. But Ben Gannon-Doak does well for the penalty and for us to go 2-1 up and see it out was good.’

No one would dispute that the display was a long way from perfect. There’s significant room for improvement ahead of the concluding group match with Switzerland on Monday.

‘We’re going through a bit of a transitional spell at the minute, so it’s not going to be all smooth sailing from the get-go,’ Graham said. ‘It’s about adjusting and trying to build on performances in every game. I think it’s going to take time.

‘It’s a different style, a different manager and we just have to keep being patient. You look at the squad now and there’s a lot of new, young players coming through. It’s just about encouraging us young boys and showing we can get a place in the squad.

‘It is going to take time but, once we get there, we’re going to do really well and compete right at the top of the game.’

Graham has been a huge success in Stoke's flying start to the Championship season

Graham does look like he’s moving in the right direction. From watching Scotland compete at the World Cup on licensed premises five months ago, he hopes he too can be the toast of the nation one day.

‘I didn’t go. It was too expensive for me,’ he explained. ‘I think I was just like everyone else, watching in the pub with their mates. It was pretty amazing and hopefully I can be part of something like that one day.

‘I wasn’t too far away (previously), I think. Steve Clarke, the former manager, told me that. It’s just about trusting myself now and hopefully getting there one day.

‘There’s been a lot of hard work and dedication which has led me to this point. I’m very grateful to a lot of people who have helped me in my career so far and just to get this chance is amazing.’

#1539. Juventus sell out Venezia game as Omonia sales pass 35,000

Juventus have sold out Sunday's Serie A home game against Venezia despite a long injury list. Strong early sales for the Europa League visit of Omonia Nicosia keep the club in line for another strong European crowd.

Juventus go into Sunday’s home game against Venezia still short of players. Eight players could miss the Venezia game. Edon Zhegrova has trained with the group and is considered available. Celik, Cambiaso, Nico Gonzalez and Kalulu remain out, Sport Mediaset reported. For Spalletti, a full home crowd arrives in the middle of a busy run of games.

General sale for the fixture opened at 3pm on Tuesday 6 October. Supporters living in the province of Venezia could buy only if they held an active Juventus Card. The fixture belongs to the 2026-27 Serie A Enilive season.

This season every Juventus match ticket is digital. Each one is managed through the Allianz Stadium App.

Season-ticket holders who cannot attend can list their seat on resale.juventus.com. The club, not the seller, sets the resale price. A few of those listings are now all that remains for supporters who missed the general sale, ANSA reported.

The season-ticket terms also reward turning up. To keep first refusal on a 2027-28 season ticket, a holder must use the seat for at least 70 per cent of matches. That means at least 13 of the 19 league games.

The Europa League has drawn big numbers to Turin this season. Against NEC, 39,308 match tickets were sold, with away fans counted separately. No away figure was released for the Rennes visit, but that section was full.

The Rennes game finished 2-2 on 22 October. That result ended Juventus’s run of two straight Europa League wins.

Omonia Nicosia are next. Bookings for the Cypriot club’s visit still trail the two earlier European crowds.

Juventus have set strict conditions for the fixture. Supporters of Cypriot nationality may buy tickets only for the away section. The club has warned that breaking UEFA rules can lead to cancelled tickets and refused entry.

Taken together, the figures are consistent with a home support that keeps buying despite the injury list. The weekend league fixture will be followed by a European night that is already well on its way to another large crowd.

Juventus host Omonia Nicosia in the Europa League on 26 November.

#1538. Marotta outlines why stadium project shows importance of Milan and Inter’s ‘forward-thinking’ ownership

Inter president Giuseppe Marotta has suggested that foreign ownership is key when it comes to modernising Italian clubs.

Last month, just before Milan’s resounding 3-1 derby win over Inter at San Siro, the two clubs unveiled the Generali Stadium. The vision is that it will become the new home for the two sides within four years, replacing San Siro which recently turned 100 years old.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

It is not just about having a new stadium for the sake of it, but rather to improve the fan experience and of course unlock commercial revenues that the current one cannot. It is one of many big plans Gerry Cardinale has to bring the Rossoneri back to the top of European football.

Beppe Marotta featured in the first episode of ‘L’impresa sportiva’, a segment on Il Sole 24 ORE’s TV program dedicated to the world of sport. He spoke about foreign ownership in Italy and the new stadium project, with his words via MilanPress.

“Football is a powerfully unifying phenomenon. After religion, I believe only sport can unite people by breaking down barriers. However, it’s also become a business. There are 12 foreign owners out of 20 in Serie A,” he began.

“On the one hand, there’s a decline, on the other, we have to ask ourselves what would have happened to football in Italy without these foreign owners. It’s no coincidence that the future stadium is a joint venture between the two Milan clubs, both of which have American owners with, frankly, very farsighted vision.

ℹ️ The capacity, the slope, the sound retention, the LED membrane and more.

🏟 @graundit with everything you need to know about the Generali Stadium 👇pic.twitter.com/3GTKIy1j0Z

— SempreMilan (@SempreMilanCom) November 12, 2026

“The stadium is the icon, the biggest investment, the most spendable, and the one everyone pays most attention to. Currently, the European club with the highest matchday revenue is Real Madrid, which closed its last financial year with around €240 million.

“We’re at €100 million, which means a gap of €140 million. The stadium must also be beautiful, welcoming, and safe. It must bring prosperity. Maximum respect for San Siro and for the emotions I felt as a child.

“But we must look forward: it is a modern stadium, which will make all its users happy, that is, the fans of both clubs. This is the home that each of us has: a home can be aesthetically beautiful, but then it is the content that strengthens it. There is nostalgia for San Siro, but evolution brings certain changes.”

#1537. Messi was a deity among Argentina’s unholy rabble

Little sorcerer calls time on playing for his country six weeks after World Cup final defeat which was marred by brutality of his team-mates

Oliver Brown leads coverage of the greatest events in sport all over the world. He has reported on multiple Olympic Games, World Cups, Ashes series and Super Bowls, plus all major golf and tennis tournaments. His awards include Sports Feature Writer of the Year and Sports Interviewer of the Year. He was named Sports Journalist of the Year in 2024 by the London Press Club. You can find him on X at @oliverbrown_tel.

Oliver Brown leads coverage of the greatest events in sport all over the world. He has reported on multiple Olympic Games, World Cups, Ashes series and Super Bowls, plus all major golf and tennis tournaments. His awards include Sports Feature Writer of the Year and Sports Interviewer of the Year. He was named Sports Journalist of the Year in 2024 by the London Press Club. You can find him on X at @oliverbrown_tel.

Lionel Messi’s haunted expression told you more than a three-page retirement statement, artfully displayed alongside a golden pen, ever could. Sobbing and desolate under a cloudless New Jersey sky, he understood that his last game for Argentina had also been among his worst.

Where four years earlier he had adorned the greatest World Cup final with two goals, he found no artistry to salvage this abomination of an encore, drifting into anonymity while his team-mates triggered a bare-knuckle brawl. No wonder he stood apart while Leandro Paredes and Nahuel Molina did their worst, preferring to absorb one more chorus of adoration from the blue-and-white disciples before forsaking the stage for good.

You could make the case that Messi, as captain of an unholy rabble that had sought only to kick lumps out of Spain, should have taken a moral lead by hauling his team-mates into line, rather than reducing himself to their level by agitating to have Marc Cucurella sent off.

And yet for 20 years, the little sorcerer stayed aloof from his nation’s most lurid antics on the pitch, establishing himself as a strangely beatific presence on whom the highest ideals could be projected. Anybody who has heard Messi’s name being chanted by 50,000 fervent Argentines would have felt it. He was as close as 21st-century sport has come to a secular deity, the object of such veneration that Pope Francis felt compelled to remind Catholics that it was sacrilegious to keep calling him God.

Today, with one agonised announcement, that glorious delirium is over, and already Argentina seems not to know what to do with itself. Pablo Giralt, a sports anchor in Buenos Aires, was unable even to speak when he heard the news live on air, while shattered young fans described how they had called their parents in tears.

Everybody had known the moment was approaching, given the finality of his exit from the final and the subsequent death of his father, Jorge, but it still triggered an unbearable sense of loss.

Messi was the force who galvanised a nation, propelling his side from the unfathomable low of defeat to Saudi Arabia at the 2022 World Cup to holding the trophy aloft 26 days later. Who could ever hope to emulate him, to detonate such joy that the team’s homecoming bus parade in the capital had to be abandoned for a helicopter ride because of the millions on the streets?

“Thank you, God, for making me Argentine,” Messi wrote in his earnest sign-off, his strength of allegiance unfailing to the end. As a veteran of 207 international matches, with his last at La Bombonera distinguished by an ecstatic ovation, he understood both the passions he unleashed among his people and the extent to which his own story became that of an entire country.

You struggled to imagine what life was like in the eye of this madness, with his every move stalked. For the wonder of Messi was that the cult went beyond borders, that the joy he inspired across six World Cups made him beloved to billions. An abiding memory of the 2022 final is of the walk back to the metro station in Doha, where thousands of Nepalese and Bangladeshi supporters, all part of the vast migrant workforce that had built the stadiums, united in “Messi, Messi” refrains even at 1am.

Messi was majestic at that tournament, so imperious in filleting Croatia in the semi-finals that Argentina’s TV reporters abandoned even the pretence of objectivity. “Truly, you made your mark in everyone’s life, and that to me is beyond winning any World Cup,” gushed Sofia Martinez of Television Publica. And when he won it all, the mark only deepened. To occupy any press box at the World Cup where Argentina were involved this summer was to see South American colleagues in “Messi 10” jerseys, helplessly in thrall to his greatness.

As a 39-year-old, he confounded every expectation, scoring a hat-trick against Algeria and breaking Miroslav Klose’s World Cup goals record. Even when engineering those implausible fightbacks against Egypt and England, he held a volatile team together with a minimum of fuss.

Lionel Messi: #FIFAWorldCup edition 🇦🇷🌟 pic.twitter.com/E2xOh3Iose

To study Messi at his last World Cup was to see a man spared the obligation to do anything off the ball. For large periods of each game, the most minutely scrutinised athlete on the planet would do little besides wander around, only to ignite when it mattered most. You saw it in the fateful semi-final with England, where, at 1-0 down, he sloped off to the right touchline as if absent-mindedly gardening. Except he was plotting his opponents’ downfall, working out the precise spots from which to unleash two sumptuous crosses and shatter English hearts.

That alchemy would elude him in the final, where Argentina’s bid for immortality brought only instant notoriety, not to mention £236,000 in fines for misconduct. Was Messi’s image hurt by his connection to the chaos? Not in the long run. Nobody likes to cling to the fact that Pelé’s swansong for Brazil was a drawn friendly with Yugoslavia, or that Diego Maradona bowed out of World Cup football by failing a drug test for ephedrine. What endure are the indelible masterpieces those players bequeathed en route.

It will be the same for Messi, a genius defined less by his ending than by the electrifying adrenalin rush he produced along the way, spanning three finals, 21 goals, and countless flourishes to take the breath away. “Thank you” was all he had left to say. And yet the gratitude, ultimately, is all ours.

#1536. “He is aware of having lost his starting place at Real Madrid”: downgrade confirmed for Vinícius Jr!

Vinícius Júnior’s status has evolved considerably at Real Madrid. Long considered an indisputable starter and one of the main faces of the Madrid project, the Brazilian winger must now deal with increased competition. According to information from José Félix Díazjournalist for A.S.the player is also perfectly aware of having lost his place in the starting lineup. An unprecedented situation for someone who had accustomed the Santiago Bernabéu to its individual differences and its decisive performances. His latest performances, less convincing than those to which he had accustomed the supporters, ultimately contributed to reshuffling the cards in the offensive hierarchy.

A particularly revealing passage of the relationship between the Portuguese technician and his player. If Mourinho does not seek to protect Vinicius from the competition nor to guarantee him a place in the eleven, the Portuguese wishes, on the other hand, to allow him to regain his best level.

This approach contrasts in particular with the relational difficulties and misunderstandings which had marked Vinicius’ previous period under Xabi Alonso. According to the Spanish daily, communication between the Brazilian and Mourinho is now excellent. The exchanges are frank, both in private and in public speaking by the Portuguese. The Madrid staff is fully mobilized to find the explosive and decisive player who had made him one of the world references in his position. For his part, Vinicius is working intensely to reverse the trend. The objective is to regain this ability to eliminate, to change matches and to constantly weigh on opposing defenses.

Real Madrid nevertheless has a certain peace of mind in this matter. Extended until June 30, 2032 last summer, Vinicius benefits from a contract which demonstrates the club’s long-term confidence. But his current figures are far from his usual standards: 12 matches played, only one goal scored and three assists. An insufficient record for a player of his caliber, even if his suspension in the championship also weighed on his season. In Madrid, no one seems to want to rush things. The club knows what the Brazilian can bring when he is playing at his best, but now expects him to demonstrate it again. You will have understood, with the recent releases of Auriverde and the rise to power of Yan Diomandé, tenure is no longer a given, it has once again become an objective.

#1535. Scotland boss Sebastien Pocognoli urges Ben Gannon-Doak to improve his end product but insists he's happy with progress of mercurial winger

Published: 17:31 EST, 14 November 2026 | Updated: 18:01 EST, 14 November 2026

Sebastien Pocognoli has backed Ben Gannon-Doak to find his killer instinct in the final third and establish himself as Scotland’s main man.

The Bournemouth youngster had an up-and-down evening in Friday’s 2-1 Nations League win over North Macedonia, getting into numerous promising positions on the right flank and winning the penalty – dispatched by John McGinn – which decided the game.

But, as has been the case throughout his Scotland career, the 21-year-old’s final ball in key moments left a lot to be desired.

Pocognoli is under no illusions that Gannon-Doak still has plenty to improve on, but insists that it won’t be long before things start to click for the talented youngster.

‘As long as he is high on the pitch and is creating one v ones I am happy,’ said the Belgian. ‘With Ben, we know that he is at a young age and needs to work on specific things.

‘On Friday, he had great opportunities. We know that he needs to improve on the end product, but he created a penalty and against Slovenia and North Macedonia away he created a number of unbelievable one v ones.

Scotland boss Sebastien Pocognoli greets Ben Gannon-Doak as he is substituted at Hampden

‘He did that last night as well. We know he can be good if we dominate the game and he can get in good positions if we control the ball. I am happy with his performance.

‘He is a young lad, just 21. Okay, he has become more mature than he was, but I believe in one moment he will have a click about decision making.

‘I believe if he is playing every game he can make many decisions. He will know that in the next game he will have to do it again.

‘If he knows that he only has to play a game every two weeks, sometimes he can think, “This is my moment”.

‘It is a process. He will become older and at some point will become relaxed in his decision making, but at this very young age what he is producing is very good.

‘I say exactly the same thing to him after training on the pitch. I say, “Ben, this is the next step”. He knows that and it is important he knows that.’

Scotland conclude their Nations League campaign in Switzerland on Monday knowing that only a victory against the group winners will be enough if they are to have any chance of leapfrogging Slovenia – currently one point better off ahead of their trip to North Macedonia – into second spot.

Pocognoli admits Gannon-Doak's end product has to improve after another frustrating show

Should that happen, Scotland would have a crack at earning promotion to League A via a play-off in March, and also crucially guarantee their place as a Pot 2 side for the upcoming Euro 2028 qualifying draw.

‘We are still alive in this competition,’ said Pocognoli, who celebrated his first win at Hampden on Friday at the third time of asking. ‘We know we have to do more than this competition. This competition is about trying to build something.

‘But it is nice to have that possibility on Monday to try to create something against one of the top 20 teams in the world.

‘We need to try to be brave. Switzerland have already qualified so let’s go there and be smart because they are a good team.

‘It is part of the process to play away against a top team. That is not something we have done yet. The approach will be different and, for me as a coach, it is a game with a lot of responsibility.’

#1534. GdS: Why Cardinale’s ‘those two million’ comment signifies Milan’s change in tact

Gerry Cardinale declared that AC Milan will alter the way they plan for preseason, but what exactly could that mean?

As La Gazzetta dello Sport write, the pile of rubble created six months ago by Milan’s defeat to Cagliari brought about a managerial and sporting revolution, and it is still going on. Cardinale continues to alter the way the club do things, hoping to evolve into an efficient and successful organisation.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

In his interview with the newspaper a few days ago, the owner extended the discussion even to the scheduling of preseason tours, stating: “Those two million for a friendly match overseas will no longer be our objective, as they were in the past.”

Beyond the actual practical implications, these words reveal a new stance: from now on, throughout the summer, sporting priorities will take precedence over financial ones. In other words, if the opportunity arises to play a friendly match outside of Europe, Amorim will be consulted.

The Rossoneri also intend to become an active participant in organising their own summer commitments. They will no longer simply put forward their availability in exchange for an offer from some tournament, but rather being the architects of their own program.

These details clearly illustrate the ownership’s shift, but in recent days there is talk of a €70m bid for Endrick, the €60m pursuit of Nicolo Tresoldi and the potential €40m acquisition of Goncalo Inacio, the money has to keep coming in.

Cardinale injected €50m in equity into the club’s coffers, earmarked for sports needs. This injection was made to make up for the loss of Champions League revenue. It’s the first time RedBird has injected cash for this purpose, with the other being €55m to buy land in San Donato.

That’s why, in this context, it’s no longer surprising when Cardinale says that ‘those €2m paid for a friendly match overseas will no longer be our goal’. The bar has been raised, with the aim of trophies being raised down the line.

#1532. CM: Morocco’s hat-trick hero leaves Amorim ‘bewitched’ – Milan’s plan for Akram Jadid

Akram Jadid’s name has been in the headlines again recently, and for good reason given his exploits on international duty.

Calciomercato.com begin a report by stating that Ruben Amorim had already made a note of Jadid’s qualities, given that he called him up to first team training at the end of August, just days before the win against Venezia.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

The coach has been ‘bewitched’ by the young talent, and it was a first opportunity for the teenager to work with the senior side. The staff also got to see exactly what level he is at, given that his scoring record gave him a reputation after netting over 700 goals in the lower levels.

Jadid represents another diamond in the youth sector for Milan, one that needs to be nurtured in the best possible way. Having risen up the age groups, he is currently a key player in Vito Michele Antonelli’s U18 team.

Last season, he was a key figure in the U15’s Scudetto victory, thanks in part to his goal in the final against Empoli. The fact he has been promoted multiple levels since says a lot about how he is through of internally.

The report described Jadid as ‘a lively, mobile left winger who enjoys constantly taking on opponents to create numerical superiority and finish, or pass (depending on the situation). He is a No.10 for his technical ability and vision, and a No.9 in the penalty area for his eye for goal’.

In this first part of the season, Jadid has made eight appearances – all as a starter – and has scored four goals against Atalanta, Inter and Lecce. He continued this good form for his country with a hat-trick for Morocco U17s in the Africa Cup of Nations qualifiers victory over Tunisia.

🇲🇦 #ACMilan youth star Akram Jadid scored a hat-trick inside five minutes for Morocco U17s ⭐️⚽⚽⚽

— SempreMilan (@SempreMilanCom) November 17, 2026

He scored three times in five minutes. The third goal was particularly impressive: after anticipating the opposing defender and pounced on a loose ball, Jadid moved inside, evaded the return of another opponent, and concluded his solo effort with a curling right-footed shot that left the goalkeeper with no chance.

What comes next? For now, Akram Jadid will continue to grow with the U18 side, but the plan is that in the coming weeks he will be tested in the Primavera, so as to be able to compete against an even higher level of opponents.

Amorim is keeping an eye on him. Given his propensity for working with young players and instilling their trust, it cannot be ruled out that Jadid could appear on the list of players called up for a Serie A match in the near future.

For now, the parallel with Francesco Camarda – another record-holder from the Rossoneri youth team – is intriguing. Milan are enjoying him, and the Italian Federation are also monitoring things, as they could try to ‘steal’ him from Morocco.

#1531. French team: Zinedine Zidane justifies his choice for Senny Mayulu

While several withdrawals have affected the French team in recent days, such as Pierre Kalulu, replaced by Saël Kumbedi, Marcus Thuram, replaced by Éli Junior Kroupi, or even Aurélien Tchouaméni, who was not to be replaced, the now confirmed withdrawal of Kylian Mbappé against Italy pushed Zinedine Zidane to call on new reinforcements. The Blues coach therefore decided to promote Senny Mayulu, initially called up with the Espoirs. The Paris Saint-Germain titi therefore joins the A group for the clash against Italy in the Nations League. Present at a press conference this Wednesday evening, on the eve of the meeting, Zinedine Zidane explained his choice.

“He can play in this position (in 9) and in the middle of the field, he does good things with Paris, he is a young player, I like his technique, what he does, he was on our lists. We do this consistently. On a list of players and Senny is with us, I’m happy with that”explained the ex-Real Madrid coach. The French technician also clarified his wishes regarding the positioning of his players: “what I want, I want to see the player, in the selection when I want to see a player, it’s in his position. We try to adapt. For Warren, this is not the case. Warren the idea is to see him in midfield in his position. » This is what is said.

#1530. Arsenal maintain perfect start but lack firepower of rivals

Bukayo Saka maintained Arsenal’s perfect start to the season, but Mikel Arteta appeared to acknowledge that the Premier League champions are in danger of leaving themselves short in attack.

There is still time for Arteta to add another forward to his squad and whether he does so or not could be important, with the transfer window closing on Tuesday night.

Having sold Leandro Trossard and with Gabriel Martinelli and Gabriel Jesus on the verge of moves away, Arsenal appear light of forward options.

Lyon winger Malick Fofana has been offered to the club, but he is an underwhelming target given Morgan Rogers and Vinícius Júnior were pursued earlier in the summer.

“We are trying to improve the squad,” Arteta, the Arsenal head coach, said. “Until Tuesday night, we’re going to try to do that. I’ve been disconnected from the world for 24 hours because I think my energy and focus has to be on the match. I will give it [my energy] now.”

Asked if he currently has enough depth in forward positions, Arteta added: “It depends if everybody is fit or not. We know that the depth has to be really big when you are fighting for four competitions. So we’re going to try to do that.”

This was an Aston Villa team there for the taking after being gutted by their Premier League rivals and still waiting for new signings to be ready to play and gel.

But Arsenal made hard work of their victory and one senses there will be more games like this if Arteta has to rely on what he has already got until at least January.

Chelsea are showing they can score goals for fun having spent £117m on Rogers. Manchester City are strengthening their firepower with the signing of Iliman Ndiaye and Bradley Barcola has joined Liverpool. Arsenal have the defence and the midfield, but not necessarily the depth of quality in forward positions of their rivals.

0.52 - Arsenal faced the fewest shots (11), the fewest shots on target (1) and allowed their opponents the lowest xG (0.52) across the first two matchdays of the Premier League season.🔒 Locked. pic.twitter.com/blSUAeqoLb

Christos Tzolis is the lone attacking signing to date and there was evidence at Villa Park that it will be a risk to rely too heavily on the Greek winger.

Tzolis had made an exciting start to his Arsenal career in the Community Shield and the first Premier League victory over Coventry City, but he had to be taken off at half-time on Monday night.

The former Club Brugge winger not only lost out to Matty Cash, but was also at the centre of Villa appeals for him to be sent off.

Tzolis had already been booked for a foul on Cash, when, in the 36th minute, he appeared to foul John McGinn as Villa broke from the edge of their own penalty area.

McGinn appealed that Tzolis should have been shown a second yellow card, but referee Jarred Gillett let the Arsenal man off the hook.

Arteta was wise to take Tzolis off at the break and his replacement, Eberechi Eze, had a hand in what proved to be Arsenal’s 59th-minute winner.

Eze slipped in Riccardo Calafiori and Saka got in front of Ian Maatsen to poke the Arsenal full-back’s low cross into the net. Saka’s goal had been the first shot on target in the game.

"It's a brilliant goal, it really is" 👏 Bukayo Saka gives Arsenal the lead at Villa Park! pic.twitter.com/aV7DA8cARL

Just before the goal, Arsenal thought they had been awarded a penalty. Ross Barkley lost possession with a sloppy pass, allowing Declan Rice to advance towards the Villa penalty area. He played the ball through for Saka and Maatsen barged into the back of the winger.

Gillett paused before pointing to the spot, but a VAR check showed that Maatsen’s foul had taken place outside the penalty area and Martin Odegaard fired the resulting free-kick wide.

The goal and the overturned penalty were pretty much it for Arsenal in terms of threatening the hosts, for whom goalkeeper Zion Suzuki made his debut. Suzuki did not have much to do with his hands, but impressed with his distribution.

It was Villa who went closest to scoring in the first half, through one of the club’s five surviving members of last season’s Europa League-winning team.

Emiliano Buendia scored Villa’s second goal in the final against Freiburg and the Argentine rattled the Arsenal crossbar with a 20-yard shot that had beaten visiting goalkeeper David Raya.

Before then, McGinn had sent a shot over Raya’s bar and into the building site where Villa are redeveloping the club’s old North Stand.

Buendia, McGinn, Cash, Pau Torres and Victor Lindelof are the only Villa players to have started the Europa League final who have not left this summer.

Defender Ezri Konsa is one of Villa’s Europa League winners to have departed and he made his Arsenal debut as a late substitute. The defender received a mixed reception, as he was first booed by some home fans but was then applauded.

Other than hitting the bar in the opening 45 minutes, Villa squandered a chance for a quick reply to Arsenal’s opener when McGinn hesitated instead of shooting after being played in by Nicolas Jackson.

Jackson lasted 71 minutes for Villa in what proved to be a promising debut. In the first half, he raced away down the right before sending the ball across the six-yard box. But there was no team-mate on hand to convert.

One of Villa’s other summer signings, Alejandro Garnacho, is yet to make an impact for his new club. The Argentine got an earful from manager Unai Emery for not being ready to go on. He eventually replaced Ross Barkley, but could not help conjure an equaliser.

This is the start Arteta wanted. But, in attacking positions, Arsenal will finish the transfer window weaker than they started it if the club are not active in the final hours of the transfer window. And that could prove costly.

We lost. We competed well. They won the league last year. We are trying to build a team but a lot of positive things [beyond] the result. How we competed. How it was progressively better. We didn’t create clear chances. Some players made fantastic debuts. Suzuki and Jackson did very good work. I think it’s the first step forward and positive for the next matches.

Accepting this result, I think we had chances to draw the match but we are in our rebuild. It is the way [ahead for us] making these changes and I say to the supporters and players that the message is there in the way we played.

To lose one match is painful but after the pain we must try to get positive things, This is the reason I am optimistic. There are 38 matches we played two. We haven’t one point but we can get better hopefully. And we will get players [Mbaye and Harwood-Bellis].

We can feel confidence because how we want to build the team again is true, to compete like today.

I think the squad we have now is how we planned with the  players we wanted.

[Are you confident you have replaced the quality that has gone?] Yes.

I’m really happy. It’s a big win. It’s a tough place to come and earn the three points but I think we deserved it.

It was a game where 11 was not enough and the finishers came in and did a magnificent job to win it. I know how tough it is to win here.

Every big team struggles against them for the past four years because they are so good. They are well coached, have great players. Great in transition. The moment you lose the ball and let them run inside they are really dangerous but I love a lot of the things I saw from my team.

Ebs [Eze] creates the action that sees us win the game, Bruno with Mikel [Merino] in midfield changed the dynamic of it, Ezri [Konsa] really composed and calm with every decision he made and then Zubi… I’m really happy with all of them.

Every game in the Premier League it’s like [you’re saying] we have to win this game. We know the level. We know how difficult it is in this league.

[Can you sign Julian Alvarez tomorrow?] I don’t know. That’s for the people upstairs.

It was a very tough match. Aston Villa’s defensive setup made things difficult for us, constantly catching us offside. We couldn’t attack as comfortably as we did last week. But as you know, sometimes one goal is enough for us. We have a very strong defence.

Today, we were great out of possession too and didn’t allow transition attacks.

I keep my targets for myself. Every week I want to be there and try decide the game as that’s what I’m in the team to do. That’s my mentality.

[Have you seen Chelsea?] I’ve seen them. [What do you think?] We’ll see on Sunday.

Jamie Carragher explains how Arsenal broke Aston Villa down for their winning goal 🔎 pic.twitter.com/CAI8zhznrJ

Arsenal host Chelsea on Sunday at 4.30pm while Villa go to Hull City at 5.30pm on Saturday. It’s too early for a must-win game for Villa who showed some positive signs tonight but they could certainly do with one.

Arsenal win with a performance of efficiency and patience that emphasises their superiority when asked to grind out a result.

John McGinnis arguing the toss with the referee about his belief that he was fouled in the box in the dying seconds. It was outside the box and if Maatsen’s ‘tackle’ wasn’t a foul, neither was Gabriel’s.

Not sure the way of refereeing that lets a lot of calls go and waits for VAR is going to enhance the game.

Maatsen tackles Bruno Guimaraes in the Villa box with an ugly lunge in which he appears to scissor him, kicking his heel with one leg before knocking the ball away with the other but the referee deems it fair and VAR lets it pass, too.

Arsenal’s game management is working well as usual until Raya goes too long and the ball bounces through to Suzuki. But when he starts a counter-attack Alysson ends it with a dive and back come Arsenal.

Maatsen slides in late on Saka down the right, bypasses the ball and crashes into his shin. Yellow card.

Aston Villa probe but Arsenal hold them 30 yards from goal and when they do slide pass down the side of a defender for Buendia to chase, Bruno is ideally positioned to cover and make the block which he celebrates as if he were Leonardo Bonucci.

Eight minutes of stoppage time are signalled by the fourth official.

Suzuki races 15 yards outside his box to head a long pass away from Havertz to McGinn. Back come Arsenal after McGinn is squeezed off the ball but Wan-Bisska wins it back with a fine tackle. He is among the best one-on-one pure defenders in the league.

Zubimendi rattles Buendia’s bones in a crunching but legal tackle.

That was Rice’s last contribution as he limps off. He is probably OK but wise to withdraw him if he has had a twinge.

Maatsen drives down the left and cuts into the box. White leans into him, Rice guides him with a rigid left arm and the rampaging left-back loses his feet. Maatsen acknowledges Rice’s fine defending when he gets back up.

Quite a few outside observers questioned why Arsenal signed Konsa. This apparent injury to Mosquera is the reason. With Saliba out for months and Timber still struggling to regain his fitness, Mosquera was the only right-sided centre-back in the squad (unless they repurposed White, who is needed at right back).

Garnacho faces up Saka after being played down the left by Buendia but his cross is blocked by the goalscorer. Raya catches the resulting corner.

McGinn wipes out Merino from behind and is deservedly booked. Moments earlier Alysson was also booked for leaving one on Gabriel after the centre-half had cleared the ball, choosing not to put on the brakes and bodychecking him instead.

Unai Emery has just gone ballistic at substitute Alejandro Garnacho.

Emery clearly wasn’t happy with Garnacho not being ready to come on and let the Chelsea loanee know about it.

And Mosquera cannot continue having overstretched so it’s a debut for the former Villa stalwart who is greeted warmly.

Suzuki saves in a one-on-one with Havertz running through from 40 yards, waiting and refusing to go down and make things easy for Havertz, sticking up a right arm to block the shot. But he may have been offside which may mitiagte it in terms of not costing Arsenal anything but he really should have beaten the keeper.

Nice pass from Merino to set the hare running.

Barkley plays a diagonal pass across the turf out to Alysson on the right and he hares round Calafiori to cross from the byline but could not get the ball past Gabriel at the near post.

Now Maatsen goes flying but this time in the Arsenal box under a challenge from White that was a duplicate of the one 30 seconds before. ‘Premier League corrupt as f---,’ sing the Villa fans, ignoring the similarities between the two incidents. The defenders’ arms made contact with the attacking players but without the force to send them sprawling.

Havertz hits the deck in the Villa penalty area when challenged by Kamara as they fought for Odegaard’s scooped dink from the right.

Bruno Guimaraes and Mikel Merino are stripped and ready to come on.

Once again, it’s Riccardo Calafiori who opens up the opposition’s defence with his off-the-ball running. He is the one player in this Arsenal team who makes genuinely unpredictable and unexpected movements.

McGinn’s combination with Jackson looks promising and the centre-forward invites him to bullock forward down the inside-right channel with a clever pass but the Villa captain is soon swamped by yellow shirts and the ball gets stuck beneath his feet.

Gary Neville makes the fair point that one of Arsenal’s most unheralded qualities is their patience. Their confidence in their rock-solid defence does not make them reckless but they are always confident of finding a way. They trust the method implicitly.

Aston Villa 0 Arsenal 1 (Saka) Mosquera has the ball 25 yards out, left of centre, he strokes it to Eze who angles a pass to Calafiori running between Cash and Lindelof. He makes it to the byline and cuts back a low cross that Saka and Maatsen both lunge at and the Arsenal winger gets there first to turn it in.

"It's a brilliant goal, it really is" 👏 Bukayo Saka gives Arsenal the lead at Villa Park! pic.twitter.com/aV7DA8cARL

Rice, Eze and Odegaard stand over it. Rive walks away and Odegaard approaches the ball with a semi-circular run-up. He whips it over the wall and about a foot wide of the left post. Suzuki was stranded but no matter.

It was outside the box. Not all that sure it was a foul either. But Arsenal will have a free-kick.

Maatsen and Saka collide as they chase a Rice pass that Saka would never reach. Seemed to be outside the box.

It has been fairly dull fare so far as two systems and structures that cede little space clash.

Lindelof rises high to meet Rice;s dipping cross from the right as Havertz, on his shoulder, was poised to pounce. He heads it straight up and Suzuki leaps to catch it.

Now Barkley picks out a diagonal to send Jackson down the left. The centre-forward reaches the 18-yard line, cuts inside and works it over to McGinn who lofts a cross over Villa’s back-post runners and out of play.

Eze did his best work from the left last season. Villa start with Barkley scoop-chipping a pass from the middle out to the left, 40 yards upfield. Maatsen runs on to it and drives past White to ram a shot into the side-netting.

Arsenal were too slow to move the ball forward in that first half, and too loose with it when they did get into promising positions. There’s a lack of urgency in their passing. I wonder if we’ll see Bruno Guimarães soon… one of the reasons they signed him was to add more quick forward passing to their play.

Signs of encouragement for Villa without creating much while Arsenal have been stymied so far by Villa’s neutering of Tzolis and the left wing. Arsenal’s right-sided trio – White, Odegaard and Saka – look the most likely to create something.

Only a minute of added time to be played. Arsenal still lacking a spark, largely because there’s a lack of precision in their forward, line-breaking passing.

Villa will be very happy with this half. Much more like their old selves in terms of structure and organisation.

Calafiori’s throw to Gabriel is picked off by Jackson down the right and he dribbles down the right. He is forced to slow down to wait for a midfield runner. When Hemmings catches up, so have three Arsenal defenders and though Jackson bends in a low, cross to the edge of the six-yard box it is about 18 inches away from Hemmings’ reach.

Calafiori goes down in the Villa box when Pau Torres uses his arm to lever him away as they tracked the flight of a cross. The referee sees nothing wring in it and neither does VAR.

Gillett takes an age to stop the play when Cash uses his body to shove Tzolis over after the winger had played a pass. Cash obviously thinks he has rattled the new signing and is keen to rough him up some more. The ref does award a free-kick but only after that daft delay.

Tzolis loses the ball on the edge of the Villa penalty area, tackled by McGinn. The captain slots a straight pass up to Buendia who tries to bend a pass into Jackson’s stride as he sprinted down the inside right channel but Gabriel read the trajectory and got there first.

Suzuki picks out McGinn with a long pass. He feeds it to Buendia who gives Hemmings a chance to chase it down the left. Arsenal shuffle over in defence so he doubles back and returns the ball to Buendia. The No 10 whips over a dipping cross looking for Barkley and Jackson but Calafiori and Raya make sure the goalkeeper wins it.

We’ve not seen much from Christos Tzolis on Arsenal’s left wing so far. He’s been excellent since joining the club this summer but he’s hardly seen the ball in this opening half an hour and he’s just been booked after losing a battle with Matty Cash.

Arsenal free-kick 30 yards out, left of centre, for a foul on Lewis-Skelly who was artfully shielding the ball. Odegaard chips to the right post but Havertz heads it back across the box rather than going for goal and Villa clear.

Cash gets the better of Tzolis again in the tackle and then Suzuki sprays a perfect 60-yard pass out to Hemmings that Gary Neville, likening it to something Ederson was capable of delivering for Man City, one of the best goalkeeper passes he has ever seen. Tzolis was booked for stopping Cash running off with the ball.

Maatsen, who could never dislodge Digne for long, has a chance now to make the position his won. He strides down the left, exploiting Rice’s positioning error but his right-foot isn’t half as good as his left and his bending effort is scuffed far too straight and easily cleared.

Saka drives down the right after a neat Odegaard, Saka, White triangle. Pau Torres races over to toe the ball behind for a corner. Saka takes and Rice flicks it on at the near post and Suzuki tips it over. No corner, though, as Gabriel had rag-dolled McGinn at the back post after the Villa captain had backed in to him and tried to stop him making a run into the middle.

“Champions of Europe, you’ll never sing that.” Villa fans poke the wound.

Arsenal are finding it difficult to play through the middle of the pitch but have found Saka in space on the right wing on a few occasions already. Villa are congesting the central areas, where Odegaard does his best work.

Calafiori picks off Kamara’s pass looking, for the third or fourth time, to play someone, usually Jackson, in behind the left-back. A minute later Calafiori challenges McGinn for a bouncing, loose ball and stoops to use his head. colliding with McGinn’s boot. Was the head low or the boot high? Arsenal think the latter but the ref sides, rightly, with McGinn.

Arsenal corner on the left. The threat inherent every time Rice is in a quadrant diminished on this occasion because Mosquera barged Cash just after Rice struck the ball. Free-kick to Villa.

Timber may be preferred by Arteta at right-back but Saka prefers White. The two have a well-grooved partnership in tersm of who underlaps and who overlaps. They never seem to get in each other’s way.

Bukayo Saka does seem to be getting a lot of time and space on the right flank.

It’s looking a risky tactic by Villa at the moment as the England international is being invited to cut in towards the penalty area.

Havertz is played down the inside-right channel in the penalty area by a cute Odegaard pass bur he blazes his shot across goal and wide of the left post. A replay shows he was offside but even so it was a lazy finish.

Kamara grabs Tzolis round the waist from behind and when the winger hits the deck, rounds him and passus to Buendia who crashes a right-foot diagonal shot on to the bar from 20 yards. The ref did not see it as a foul despite Arsenal’s protestations but had it gone in it would have given VAR a dilemma.

Worth keeping an eye on Aston Villa midfielder George Hemmings tonight.

He is only a teenager and has emerged from Villa’s academy, but Unai Emery is already a huge fan.

Hemmings produced a highly promising performance in the Super Cup against Paris Saint-Germain earlier this month.

Suzuki misjudges the flight of Rice’s typically menacing corner and flaps at it but his defenders and an offside flag leave him without egg on his face.

McGinn stops Calafiori down the left then gives the ball straight to Tzolis. The Greece winger opens his body and passes to Lewis-Skelly who shoots with his right foot from the left of the 18-yard line. Cash slides in to block the shot and it loops over the bar for a corner.

Hemmings uses his strength to hold off Ben White and shift the ball inside to McGinn who wraps his left instep around a shot and wafts it into building site behind Raya’s goal.

Ibrahim Mbaye and Taylor Harwood-Bellis are in the directors’ box watching the game. Villa don’t look like a hastily assembled team.

Suzuki knocks the ball long with his left foot, looking for Jackson but the ball spins away from him to Raya who boots it back upfield. McGinn pounces on it, turns past Rice and plays Cash in down the right. He crosses towards the near post and Mosquera hooks it clear.

Arsenal kick off with Odegaard spinning and trying to play Saka in down the right as they defend the empty North Stand end. The ball skids off the turf and Saka can’t trap it. The ball goes out for a Villa throw-in.

Who dies in the summer and played for both clubs.

Arsenal are in fact in yellow and navy. My mistake.

Villa in claret and blue with a twist, the shorts are blue for the first time since, I think 2001. Arsenal are in yellow and black. Leeds, like Arsenal, have traditionally worn yellow and blue as their away strip but have been shunted into yellow and black as well by Adidas this season.

There are a few guys standing in the North Stand with hard hats on, and it appears they are on ball retrieval duty.

They will be on red alert for any wayward shots that land in the empty stand.

Warm reception for Ezri Konsa from Villa’s fans as he walked back to the tunnel with Arsenal’s substitutes.

Konsa joined Arsenal last week for £51m, ending a spell of seven years at Villa Park.

Wonder if the likes of Morgan Rogers and Emiliano Martinez will get a similar reception when they return here with Chelsea.

Aston Villa  Suzuki; Cash, Lindelof, Torres, Maatsen; Kamara, Barkley; McGinn, Buendía, Hemmings; Jackson. Substitutes  Bizot, Mings, Ruggeri, Garnacho, Abraham, Bogarde, Wan-Bissaka, Edward, Lynch.

Arsenal  Raya; White, Mosquera, Gabriel, Calafiori; Lewis-Skelly, Rice; Saka, Odegaard, Tzolis; Havertz. Substitutes  Arrizabalaga, Hincapié, Eze, Gyokeres, Konsa, Madueke, Merino, Zubimendi, Guimaraes.

Zion Suzuki is one of two debuts for Aston Villa tonight and there is a genuine buzz of excitement around the Japan international.

Suzuki was signed from Parma for £30m as the replacement for Emiliano Martinez and arrives with a stellar reputation.

He’s got big boots – and gloves – to fill, but Unai Emery is convinced he will become a future star at Villa Park.

The other debutant is record £65m signing Nicolas Jackson, who joined last week from Chelsea.

Good evening. Yes, the first match was not as planned but we must keep going forward. Today we are playing our first home match and I am looking forward. We need to try as soon as possible to get our best individuals fit for a good performance. And today is a good match for us. Ir is difficult but always with our supporters here we feel comfortable and confident. Hopefully we can transmit our positive energy to our supporters.

We lost the first game but it is not a [team full of rookies]. We have experienced players. They play with energy and know how we want to play. We have to adapt with Suzuki but we have confidence [in him]. Jackson, the striker, and other players, George Hemmings, he is young but played fantastically in pre-season. He knows how we want to play.

Today is a challenge but I’m really looking forward to how the players will respond collectively, individually. We know we are changing things but no excuses. We have to perform today, we have to try to adapt the new players, to build our team to get their best today.

I am positive and I am optimistic. The players are ready.

Aston Villa are in a transition period and rebuilding on and off the field.

Unai Emery’s 2.0 have been under construction all summer and there could be 10 new signings in by tomorrow morning.

Villa have of course lost six of the starting XI from last season’s Europa League final, with Morgan Rogers, Ollie Watkins, Ezri Konsa, Youri Tielemans, Emiliano Martinez and Lucas Digne all departing this summer.

The North Stand at Villa Park, which faces the iconic Holte End, is also under renovation and closed down for tonight’s game.

It could be a bit quieter tonight but there is still a mood of optimism among Villa fans, despite such a summer of change.

We have had a real block of training sessions to work on things and prepare for this game in the right way.

We will have time to make changes throughout the game [on why he has picked an unchanged team]. They did really well [against Coventry] and for the game we expect [tonight] they have the right qualities to hurt them and that’s how we start.

They have that [upheaval in personnel] but they have been with Unai for a long time, they are a super well-coached team and we know how tough it is always to come here. We are very conscious of that but also very ambitious.

That’s the way we want to play [with aggression] constantly from the first minute, to suffocate the opponent and be better than them.

[Does it being your 250th Arsenal Premier League game add something special to it?] Just to win [makes it special].

Good evening and welcome to live coverage of the Premier League match between Aston Villa and Arsenal from Villa Park. The champions travel to the team that finished fourth last season in buoyant mood and form despite some misgivings within their fanbase about their recruitment this summer.

It amounts so far to making Pier Hincapié‘s loan into a proper transfer, revamping the left wing with Christos Tzolis replacing Leandro Trossard and Gabriel Martinelli, upgrading options in central midfield by buying Bruno Guimarães and selling Cristian Norgaard – and signing Ezri Konsa from today’s opponents to give them the greatest elite defensive depth that I can recall at club since Manchester City’s Treble winners had Kyle Walker, Ruben Dias, John Stones, Nathan Aké, João Cancelo, Aymeric Laporte, Manuel Akanji, Rico Lewis and Sergio Gómez on the books at the same time.

Villa, by contrast, have endured a turbulent summer of trading with the departures of Europa League winners Morgan Rogers, Youri Tielemans, Lucas Digne, the aforementioned Konsa, Ollie Watkins and Emi Martínez, raising, along with other departures, more than £315m. They have spent about £180m to remodel the team though Johan Manzambi, who is injured, and João Gomes, who is suspended after his red card in the 4-0 defeat by Brighton, are absent tonight.

We can expect to see Zion Suzuki, Matteo Ruggeri and hopefully Nicolas Jackson and Leon Goretzka who have been registered in time to play, plus the loan signings Aaron Wan-Bissaka and Alejandro Garnacho. Still to come are the pending purchases of Taylor Harwood-Bellis and Ibrahim Mbaye in a process that emphasises how profoundly Villa are invested in and dependent upon their manager, Unai Emery.

After so much upheaval, it would be foolish to set much store on Villa’s 2-1 victory last season, sealed by Emi Buendía’s winner in the fifth minute of stoppage time. Arsenal barely broke sweat in blowing Man City away in the Community Shield and cakewalked to victory over Coventry in the league’s opening fixture. His past work suggests Emery will be able to forge another formidable side from his talented new squad but this match feels two months too soon for him against his old club.

#1528. John McGinn warns Tartan Army it might take 18 MONTHS for Scotland to click into gear under new boss Pocognoli

By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER

Published: 17:42 EST, 14 November 2026 | Updated: 18:03 EST, 14 November 2026

Amid the clamour for a change at the helm following another poor showing at a major tournament, it was easy to lose sight of the reality of the situation.

Steve Clarke didn’t crash and burn in the US because a raft of world-class talents failed to turn up on the biggest stage. It happened primarily because a limited squad was unable to outperform two top-ten nations in Brazil and Morocco who could call upon infinitely superior footballers.

Sebastian Pocognoli has since arrived on the scene having earned a stellar reputation from his title success with Union Saint-Gilloise and his less feted spell at Monaco. But he has not come armed with a magic wand.

In opening the door to a string of fresh faces and advocating the more attacking approach which so many craved, the turbulence he’s experienced to date should only have been expected.

Limited by both the standard of players who are eligible for Scotland and the time he has to work with them, only the blissfully naïve would have seen his appointment as a quick fix.

While there were some positives to be taken from the game with North Macedonia – primarily the result – it’s likely the nation will have to endure more short-term pain for long-term gain.

Scotland boss Sebastien Pocognoli greets his players after a satisfactory evening at Hampden

This was always going to take time, perhaps, in the view of John McGinn, more than many may have imagined.

‘The manager’s got a great reputation, a good record at both places he’s been,’ said the Aston Villa captain. ‘The most important thing now in football is individuals don’t win you games. It’s unity, teamwork and everyone being on the same page.

‘You see how successful clubs and successful countries do it. And we want to be one of them.

‘It’s not going to happen overnight. There’s a lot to learn but we did create big chances against North Macedonia where we could have scored three, four or five and it could be a different story.

‘But this isn’t something that gets fixed in March or even next September. It will start to build over the next 18 months.’

If that predicted time frame might raise an eyebrow or two, McGinn makes no apology for it. Call it managing expectations from the midfielder if you please. But without a degree of patience from the Tartan Army, he feels Pocognoli’s ideas won’t take root.

‘I understand it’s frustrating,’ he added. ‘It’s freezing and you want to see four, five, six goals, but the balance has got to be there.

McGinn sends his penalty home to give Scotland a deserved lead against North Macedonia

‘They’re entitled to their opinion, but there’s got to be a mixture of patience.

‘The supporters are entitled to say whatever they like. But just as long as they hurl anything they want to shout at the experienced boys and just let the young ones flourish and try and settle into the team.’

Give credit where it’s due. With Clarke accused of causing stagnation by selecting the same old faces, Pocognoli has capped five players for the first time while recalling the likes of Oli McBurnie.

The sages in the stands can’t have it both ways. If the squad was going to evolve, it was never going to be a smooth ride.

‘I think the young players are starting to show more now,’ McGinn stressed. ‘Luke Graham on Friday night, I thought he was brilliant. It’s not easy playing in the middle of a back three. He’s been waiting for his chance and the manager’s shown that if you deserve your chance you’re going to get put in there.

‘We’ve got so many players that can step up and they will. We just need to show that belief and take it to the pitch.’

Even in victory, McGinn doesn’t dispute that there is significant scope for improvement. He’s convinced, however, that this will all come good in the end.

McGinn insists it's vital the entire Scotland squad buy into the methods of manager Pocognoli

‘We need to play slightly better,’ he said. ‘We know that, but we’re going through a period which I’ve been used to at club level, a lot of changes, a lot of detail that we need to try and remember and get used to.

‘And it’s about sticking at it. We’re keen to play a style of football that’s not easy but is going to get bums off seats. It’s important that everyone believes in it because if one person drops off or doesn’t believe in it, that’s when it all starts to fall apart.’

Friday was another memorable night on a personal level for McGinn. Having broken the tension with the opener only to see North Macedonia level, he held his nerve to put Scotland back from the penalty spot.

The brace put him on 24 international goals, now within six of Denis Law and Kenny Dalglish. But all of that is for another day.

‘It feels a bit strange, but at the minute that’s gone to the back burner,’ he stressed. ‘I had a wee chat with Scott (McTominay) about the penalties. I was designated penalty taker but, to be fair, he’s not missed one I don’t think in his career.

‘So, we had a wee chat and I think we both said the most important thing was just no matter who hit it, hit the back of the net.’

McGinn is eyeing three points against Switzerland in St Gallen to close the campaign on a high

Tomorrow, the equation is clear. To finish second in the Nations League group and secure a place in pot two for the Euro draw, Scotland must beat the Swiss and hope that Slovenia don’t beat North Macedonia.

Even if everything clicks for Pocognoli’s side, it will be the tallest of orders.

‘Difficult,’ said McGinn. ‘I know they drew on Friday night (with Slovenia) but they’ve got a couple of players back that they were missing last time.

‘It is a tough one but we want to be competing against these teams away from home. It’s not going to be perfect for a while, but we’ll stick at it.’

#1527. Ligue 1: PSG provides the essentials against Troyes and consolidates its leadership position

Four days after their performance at Villarreal in the Champions League (0-6), Paris Saint-Germain (1st) returned to the Parc des Princes for the reception of Troyes (16th) in Ligue 1. Deprived of Achraf Hakimi (rest) and Maghnes Akliouche (injured), Luis Enrique launched Warren Zaire-Emery at right-back, Senny Mayulu in the middle with Fabián Ruiz and Vitinha, and Mika Godts alongside Désiré Doué and Ferran Torres. Opposite, ESTAC was coming off an important success for confidence against Le Mans (2-0), but had to hope for a miracle to leave Paris with the three points.

The Parisians quickly took control of the meeting. After a first alert with this shot from Senny Mayulu diverted onto the bar by the Trojan goalkeeper (5th), PSG opened the scoring. After having already called on Hillel Konaté two minutes earlier, Illya Zabarnyi perfectly headed a cross from Mayulu to open the scoring (39th, 1-0). Just before half-time, Ferran Torres had the opportunity to make the break, but the 2026 world champion lost his one-on-one against the Burkinabè goalkeeper (45th+1).

Returning from the locker room, Renaud Ripart faced Matvey Safonov, but his attempt did not find the target (56th). PSG then had several opportunities to make the break, notably by Zaire-Emery, whose header from a cross from Doué narrowly missed (61st), then Ferran Torres, again defeated by an excellent Hillel Konaté (69th). The Parisians finally trembled until the end, when Maronnier thought he equalized after a corner, before finally being flagged offside (84th).

Despite overall domination and several clear chances, Paris Saint-Germain was therefore content with the bare minimum against Troyes. After its festival in C1, the Capital club won its 11th victory in a row in all competitions and its seventh success in the league to increase its lead at the top of Ligue 1 before the international break. For its part, Troyes remains a barrier and could enter the relegation zone at the end of this 10th day.

#1525. Architecture of a portal complex embedded in the poxvirus core

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

We’re sharing this article early to provide faster access to peer-reviewed, accepted research. It is citable and carries a permanent DOI. This version is subject to further edits and will be replaced automatically by the final Version of Record. All legal disclaimers apply.

Gene transcription within the viral core is a distinctive feature of poxvirus replication. Following entry into the cytoplasm, the poxvirus core dissociates from the lateral bodies and undergoes expansion, functioning as a compartment for early transcription1. However, how molecules are exchanged between the viral core and the host cytoplasm remains poorly understood. Here, using cryo-electron tomography and sub-tomogram averaging, we determine the structures of the portal complex and its central pore on the vaccinia virus core at 6.7 Å and 4.4 Å resolution, respectively. Guided by structural predictions and experimental density, we identify three viral proteins, E8, E6 and L3, as the principal components of the pore and construct a structural model of their organization. The pore contains a narrow, positively charged constriction formed by conserved lysine residues in L3, substitutions of which impair viral gene expression and propagation. The dimensions and electrostatic properties of the channel are consistent with a potential role in molecular exchange across the core wall. Together, our findings establish a structural framework for understanding the organization and potential function of the poxvirus portal complex.

#1524. 'Dad, we are not walking out of the match. It's my first time in Old Trafford!' - An afternoon with my 10-year-old inside the Theatre of Screams for Carrick's last stand

Published: 18:49 EST, 14 November 2026 | Updated: 18:49 EST, 14 November 2026

‘Mate, we are walking out in the 21st minute to protest 21 years of the Glazers. Will you join us?’ he asks earnestly, handing me a leaflet that announces: ‘Enough is Enough! Empty Old Trafford! Leave the stadium in the 21st minute. 21 years of failed ownership. Glazers OUT! Ineos OUT!’

More than 70,000 spectators leaving their seat and walking out of the stadium in the 21st minute have been quite the statement, especially live on Sky Sports.

But as admirable as Saeed TV’s aim is (I discover later he is some sort of youtuber), it’s hard to see gain any traction.

‘Dad, we are not walking out of the match. It’s my first time in Old Trafford,’ I am told as we continue to meander up Matt Busby Way, a declaration from my 10-year-old that causes a fair bit of mirth among the crowd.

Mate, we are walking out in the 21st minute to protest 21 years of the Glazers. Will you join us?’

‘What’s wrong with the owners anyway?’ Dan enquires innocently, which leads to a bind.

How deep down the rabbit-hole should I go with my ten-year-old on his first visit to the Theatre of Dreams.

It’s probably not the time or place to try and explain leveraged buyouts and how much debt the Glazers have saddled the club with, £1.2 billion at the last count while taking millions out of it in dividends. Do I need to go further back and talk about Rock of Gibraltar’s unexpected success on the track and the concept of stud fees?

‘They are not putting enough money into the team and taking loads of money out of the club,’ is all I offer.

‘When Manchester City need a midfielder, they can buy Elliot Anderson and Enzo Fernandez while United have to make do with someone who was sitting on Chelsea’s bench.’

He doesn’t look convinced that’s much of a reason to walk out of a football but as the cathedral of consumerism that is the Manchester United megastore has appeared, he forgets about United’s disastrous ownership model – for now, at least.

During his doomed attempt to coax Jurgen Klopp to Old Trafford around 2014, Ed Woodward apparently told him that United was the sporting version of Disneyland.

And to be sardined inside the megastore in the couple of hours before kick-off, you have to accept that the much-maligned former CEO may have been right about one thing.

Think Arnott’s a couple of days before Christmas, just with a lot more people. You even need to pass through airport-like security before even entering and spend your dosh.

One of the common refrains among United supporters is why are the Glazers holding onto the club when they don’t even seem to care.

Thirty seconds inside the megastore on match-day and you realise why the Americans are so keen to hold onto the asset they’re bleeding dry – and they probably care a great deal.

Dan gets obligatory photo at statue of United's holy trinity, a moment he will look back on

Even with the team languishing in the relegation zone, having won a single league game all season, people are keen to spend, spend, spend.

I see people wandering around with five or six different shirts, from different eras (I did succumb and bought Dan the black shirt from 95-96 season, because it reminds me of Eric Cantona, Roy Keane and better times!)

You can get a photo with a replica of a Premier League trophy. That’s just £10. Or Lego sets of Old Trafford or the Munich clock.

That will just set you back £25.  For many in this shop, it seems allowing the club to empty their wallet is as much a part of the day as the actual football.

There are other parts of the ritual, which remain and have yet to be infected by the poisonous atmosphere around the club – and remind the three dads bringing their kids to Old Trafford for the first time of better days.

Such as curry chips and battered sausage from Lou Macari’s chipper. And the customary photo in front of the statue of the holy trinity of Best, Law and Charlton.

The megastore was the one place that seemed immune to the toxicity in the air. Once outside again and all that could be heard was the moans and groans, mainly because Shea Lacey wasn’t starting.

Coming here since the 1990s, we have seen the skyline of Manchester transformed as it became a sleek, modern city. It seems the one place that hasn’t changed is Old Trafford. It has remained the same.

Stuck in time. It looked sleek and modern in 1999, but now there is a tired, decrepit feel to the stadium – and not just because of the leaking roof. It could do with a lick or two of paint.

Stuck in time. It looked sleek and modern in 1999, but now there is a tired, decrepit feel to the stadium

No wonder Big Sir Jim is determined to plough ahead with his plans to make a crudely-designed circus tent ‘the Wembley of the North.’ Not that there is anyone inside Old Trafford of the same mind.

Senne Lammens has just trotted onto the field with Tom Heaton and Karl Darlow to do their pre-match warm-up when the chants start, telling Jim Ratcliffe he can stick his new stadium up his posterior.

It is a weird atmosphere, with all the chanting against the owners – both Glazers and Ineos – and nothing being sung in support of the players.

As my friend points out it must be so difficult for the team to show the best of themselves when things are this toxic in the stadium.

Dan has been to the Jodi Stand enough times on a Friday night to know there is plenty of choice and crude language at football matches, but still I nearly felt at covering his ears at some of the stuff being sung in Old Trafford last Sunday, especially that directed at CEO Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox.

We had hoped that things might have been different when the game kicked off, but within a minute, Aston Villa had scored.

And three minutes later, they had scored again when Lammens fumbled Alysson’s shot into Nicolas Jackson’s path. Maybe walking out in the 21st minute wasn’t such a bad idea.

The crowd’s ire had gone from the owners to the players now, with a sustained chant of ‘You are not fit to wear the shirt.’ United did rally and by half-time, it was 2-2. But the mood was still dismal as we queued for a quick beer.

The 1958 Group had asked fans not to buy booze, another protest against the owners. But it seemed nobody was paying much attention to that.

One of the issues at United is that there seem to be too many splintered fan groups – there is also ClaimBackUnited and Fan Coalition ’58 – as well as Saeed TV, who seemed to be on his own solo run.

We didn’t feel bad about ignoring the booze ban, as everyone was doing it. And within a couple of minutes of the second-half, we saw the reason why. You need to fortify yourself to watch Diogo Dalot try to defend.

For much of the second-half, it seemed like Michael Carrick’s brief tenure was going to peter out in a forgettable defeat, as Villa seemed to manage the game perfectly.

Dan and his friends were growing frustrated, pointing out the players weren’t doing what their coaches tell them to do on a weekly basis, leading me to conclude that maybe my son’s under-11 side are better-coached than United.

The last on-pitch act of Carrick's tenure

And then there was the chaotic and crazy final few minutes in stoppage-time. And a draw that came out of nowhere and was celebrated like a victory.

That was the thing. Even though the mood inside the stadium was toxic for most of the game, even though the team were two down inside four minutes and the season has been a disaster, everyone still came away from Old Trafford, happy and with a smile on their face.

Only football can do that. More than that, perhaps only Manchester United – despite everything – can do that.

#1522. GdS: Two games, one shot and an angry team-mate – ‘nightmare’ for Ramos extends to Portugal

AC Milan welcomed back a rejuvenated Goncalo Ramos after the last international break, but they will not do so this time.

As La Gazzetta dello Sport write, Ramos is finding himself ‘trapped in a nightmare season’, which is now also taking its toll on him for the national team too. As a reminder, he scored three goals in three starts (against Norway, Denmark and Norway again) during the September-October break.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

This allowed him to put his struggles behind him for a couple of weeks, but things are now getting tough with the Seleção as well. Last Saturday – in a 4-1 defeat against Denmark – he finished the match without even touching the ball in the penalty box.

It was frighteningly similar to the isolation seen at Milan, and the problem is that his numbers didn’t improve even in Wales. Portugal won 3-2 but not only did the former PSG man not get his name on the scoresheet, he also didn’t participate in any of the goals directly.

His numbers in the 59 minutes he was on the pitch: 1 shot attempted (a header from Neto’s pass from the left in the 47th minute), 4/7 successful passes, 11 touches, and 1 unsuccessful dribble. The story of a striker who is not involved.

That’s not all, either. Gonçalo also angered Bruno Fernandes. It happened during a counter-attack, with the Portuguese captain breaking down the left and crossing low, expecting Ramos to be there. Gonçalo had stopped though, and Fernandes’s reprimand was inevitable.

The two would later have another exchange at the end of the match, with Bruno reminding his team-mate – who was disappointed to be brought off after less than an hour – of the responsibility of replacing a giant like Cristian Ronaldo. Oh, and Bruno Fernandes has been linked today, by the way.

In short, Goncalo Ramos is ‘twisted in a spiral he can’t seem to escape’. After the game in Cardiff last night, he has reached 661 minutes without a goal for club and country. The last one was exactly a month ago, on October 18th against Atalanta.
