a, Characteristics of the two studies. b, Test–retest ICC(2,1) for bilateral, left and right regional volumes (two-way random-effects, absolute agreement, single measurement). Points are ICC estimates. Bars show 95% confidence intervals computed by irr::icc. n = 8 independent participants, each scanned twice (16 scans, paired measurements). Red indicates ICC < 0.4. c, Pearson correlation heatmap of hypothalamic structure volumes and age at MRI in cognitively normal, amyloid-negative participants (n = 165 independent participants). Blue and red indicate positive and negative correlations, respectively. Two-sided Pearson tests used Benjamini–Hochberg (BH) correction across all pairwise correlations (*adjusted P < 0.05, **adjusted P < 0.01, ***adjusted P < 0.001). d, Age–volume Pearson r in cognitively normal, amyloid-negative participants, analysed as pooled (black, n = 165), CBA (orange, n = 91) and AMBR (blue, n = 74) samples. Two-sided Pearson tests used BH correction across 26 age–volume correlations per analysis. Filled circles indicate adjusted P < 0.05, open circles non-significance. e, Associations of age, female sex and intracranial volume with subregion volumes in AMBR, CBA and pooled participants. Points show Gaussian GLM coefficients. Bars show unadjusted approximate 95% confidence intervals (estimate ± 1.96 × s.e.). Every regional model used 107 AMBR, 209 CBA or 316 pooled independent participants. Models included age, sex, cognition, amyloid-β, cognition × amyloid-β and intracranial volume, plus study in pooled models. Two-sided t-tests used 100, 202 and 308 residual degrees of freedom, respectively. BH correction covered 26 regions per predictor and cohort. Exact estimates, intervals, t statistics, degrees of freedom and raw/adjusted P are in Supplementary Tables 2–4. In the figure panels, AN denotes the arcuate nucleus (ARC in the main text) and DM denotes the dorsomedial hypothalamic nucleus (DMH in the main text).

a, Pearson correlation heatmap of extrahypothalamic volumes and age at MRI (n = 458 independent participants). Blue and red indicate positive and negative correlations, respectively. Two-sided Pearson tests used Benjamini–Hochberg (BH) correction across unique pairwise correlations within the matrix (*adjusted P < 0.05, **adjusted P < 0.01, ***adjusted P < 0.001). b, Age–volume Pearson correlations in the pooled cohort (n = 458 independent participants), CBA (n = 256) and AMBR (n = 202). Two-sided Pearson tests used BH correction across all 26 regional age–volume correlations within each cohort. Filled circles indicate adjusted P < 0.05. Open circles indicate adjusted P ≥ 0.05. c, Forest plots of Gaussian GLM coefficients for hypothalamic (top) and extrahypothalamic (bottom) volumes, ordered by coefficient estimate. Points show fitted coefficients and bars show unadjusted approximate 95% confidence intervals (estimate ± 1.96 × SE). n = 316 independent participants in every model, with covariates as in Fig. 1c. Two-sided coefficient t-tests used 308 residual degrees of freedom. BH adjustment covered all eight coefficients, including the intercept, within each regional model. Point color and size indicate adjusted significance. d, Age, female sex and intracranial volume coefficients for extrahypothalamic structures. Points show Gaussian GLM coefficients and bars show unadjusted approximate 95% confidence intervals (estimate ± 1.96 × SE). Every regional model used 107 AMBR, 209 CBA or 316 pooled independent participants. Models included age, sex, cognition, amyloid-β, cognition × amyloid-β and intracranial volume, plus study in the pooled analysis. Two-sided coefficient t-tests used 100, 202 and 308 residual degrees of freedom, respectively. P values were BH-adjusted across 26 regions separately for each predictor and cohort. e, Body mass index (BMI) associations in AMBR-only Gaussian GLMs. Points show BMI coefficients per SD of BMI and bars show unadjusted approximate 95% confidence intervals (estimate ± 1.96 × SE). n = 174 independent participants in each regional model. Models adjusted for age, sex, cognition, amyloid status, cognition × amyloid status, HbA1c, Epworth sleepiness score and intracranial volume. Two-sided coefficient t-tests used 164 residual degrees of freedom. BH adjustment covered all ten model coefficients, including the intercept, within each regional model. Exact results for all panels are in Supplementary Tables 2–4. In the figure panels, AN denotes the arcuate nucleus (ARC in the main text) and DM denotes the dorsomedial hypothalamic nucleus (DMH in the main text).

a, PCA of 25 hypothalamic and extrahypothalamic structure volumes (n = 458 participants). Scatter plots are colored by eight covariates: age, sex, amyloid-β status, cognitive status, intracranial volume (ICV), total brain volume (TBV), study and amyloid days. Three variants are shown: raw volumes (top, PC1 = 44.2%, PC2 = 14.4%), fully residualized for age, sex, ICV, TBV and study (middle, PC1 = 27.6%, PC2 = 13.1%), and partially residualized for sex, ICV, TBV and study (bottom, PC1 = 27.4%, PC2 = 13.9%). b–c, PC1 and PC2 loadings from raw (b) and fully residualized (c) PCA. Bars are red for negative loadings and teal for positive loadings. d, Changes in PC1 (left) and PC2 (right) loadings from raw (orange) to fully residualized (green) PCA, shown as dumbbell plots ordered by magnitude of change. e, Associations of PC1–PC5 scores with nine covariates in raw and partially residualized PCA. Continuous covariates were tested using two-sided Pearson correlations, with r2 as effect size. Categorical covariates were tested using omnibus one-way ANOVA F-tests, with η2 as effect size and an upper-tail F reference distribution. P values were Benjamini–Hochberg (BH)-adjusted across 45 PC–covariate tests separately for each PCA variant. n = 458 participants, with data available for cognitive status in 422, amyloid-β status in 340, CogDays in 441 and AmyloidDays in 358. *Adjusted P < 0.05, **adjusted P < 0.01, ***adjusted P < 0.001. f, Regional volume versus age in n = 181 independent male participants. Each point represents one participant, colored by combined cognitive and amyloid status (black, missing status). Black LOESS curves estimate conditional mean volume. Shading shows pointwise 95% confidence intervals for the fitted curves, rather than between-participant standard deviations. g, Regional volume distributions after nearest-neighbor propensity-score matching of AD and cognitively unimpaired, amyloid-negative participants on sex and age. The pooled comparison includes 24 AD participants (18 men, 6 women) and 24 matched controls (16 men, 8 women). Center lines show medians, box bounds the 25th and 75th percentiles, and whiskers the most extreme observations within 1.5 × the interquartile range of the box bounds. Dots represent individual participants, including observations beyond the whiskers. Duplicate outlier symbols are suppressed. h, ROC curves from class-balanced logistic regression with five-fold stratified cross-validation, using 13 hypothalamic subregion volumes or total hypothalamic volume to predict cognitive impairment (n = 422 participants, 140 impaired, 282 unimpaired), amyloid positivity (n = 340, 63 positive, 277 negative) and AD status (n = 316, 24 AD, 292 others). AUCs are mean ± standard deviation across five folds. The subregion model had a higher mean AUC for all three outcomes. No formal comparison was performed. i, Univariate ROC curves predicting AD status from 25 hypothalamic and extrahypothalamic structures and total hypothalamic volume (n = 316 participants, 24 AD, 292 others), sorted by descending AUC. The arcuate nucleus (AN; ARC in the main text), fornix (fx), paraventricular nucleus (Pa) and ventromedial nucleus (VM) were the strongest predictors. When lower volume predicted AD (indicated by “−”), scores were sign-inverted before ROC calculation.

a, Donor metadata. The table summarizes condition, age, Braak stage, APOE genotype, amyloid-β status, postmortem delay (PMD), RNA integrity number (RIN) and time of death for each donor. Accompanying heatmaps show donors clustered by pathology metrics (left) and quality metrics (right), with annotation bars indicating condition, time of death, pathology and quality. b, UMAP showing nuclei from this study embedded within a reference atlas of 25 million publicly available human brain cells, colored by major cell type and condition. c, UMAP of the integrated dataset following scVI batch correction, with nuclei colored by condition, batch, individual, and inclusion of the Siletti et al. dataset. d, Boxplots of the per-tissue-sample mean number of genes detected per nucleus, stratified by cell type and condition. Each tissue sample is one hypothalamic subregion from one donor. The center line is the median, box bounds are the 25th and 75th percentiles, and whiskers extend to the most extreme observations within 1.5 × the interquartile range of the box bounds. Observations beyond the whiskers are shown as points. CTL and AD contain seven donors each (AD includes the familial case). Young reference samples derive from three donors, except young epithelial cells, which derive from one donor. In cell-type order neuron, epithelial, endothelial, ependymal, OPC, astrocyte, fibroblast, oligodendrocyte, microglia, and leukocyte, n (CTL/AD/young tissue samples) is 21/21/24, 8/4/2, 21/21/19, 19/17/19, 21/21/24, 21/21/24, 21/21/23, 21/21/24, 21/21/22 and 21/21/19. The epithelial samples come from four CTL and three AD donors. These are descriptive summaries, and no inferential test is shown. e, Boxplots of the per-tissue-sample mean UMI count per nucleus, with the same samples and group sizes as d. Boxplot elements are as in d. The y-axis is logarithmic. No inferential comparison is presented. f, Stacked bar plots showing cell-type composition for samples from each hypothalamic subregion (SCN, MN, and ARC). g, Bar plot quantifying the total number of nuclei for each cell type in the final dataset.

Selected significantly enriched Hallmark (top) and Gene Ontology biological process (GO:BP; bottom) pathways from GSEA. The analysis was performed on genes ranked by their signed model weights. The dot plot shows the top pathways for the all-cell model and for each of the five cell-type-specific models. The x-axis represents the absolute NES, dot size represents the number of genes in a pathway, and color indicates significance (−log10[FDR]).

a, Top row: violin plots displaying significant DEGs across specific major cell types (endothelial cells, microglia, and OPCs) from snRNA-seq, comparing CTL and AD individuals. Bottom row: boxplots illustrating the normalized log2 abundance of the corresponding significant differentially abundant proteins (DAPs) in CSF, comparing healthy controls (HC) with AD patients. Statistical significance with BH correction is indicated by asterisks (*P < 0.05, **P < 0.01, ***P < 0.001, ****P < 0.0001). b, UMAP projections illustrating the expression scores for three senescence-related and three NFT-related gene signatures across all nuclei. c, Violin plots comparing the expression scores of three NFT-related signatures across major cell types. Per-sample mean UCell scores for the NFT Orr signature were higher in AD than control (Wilcoxon rank-sum test on 18 AD versus 21 control samples, BH-adjusted across cell types: microglia P = 0.037, OPC P = 0.025). d, Violin plots showing the expression of key senescence-related genes (CDKN1A, canonical; CALR, responses; SOD2, initiators) across major cell types. Pseudobulk edgeR-LRT false discovery rate (FDR) is indicated by asterisks (*P < 0.05, **P < 0.01, ***P < 0.001, ****P < 0.0001). e–f, Module scores for the mTOR signaling (e) and extracellular matrix (ECM; f) gene sets, comparing control and AD donors at the sample level, stratified by cell type. Scores were computed using Seurat’s AddModuleScore (background-corrected mean expression relative to randomly sampled control gene sets matched by expression level). Each point represents the mean per-sample score for a given cell type (minimum 10 cells per sample). Boxes show median and IQR; whiskers extend to 1.5 × IQR. Brackets indicate pairwise comparisons with BH-adjusted significance (Wilcoxon rank-sum test).

a, Split UMAP embeddings of hypothalamic microglia/macrophage nuclei by group: young, 3,213 nuclei (3 donors), CTL, 24,648 (7 donors), AD, 20,087 (6 donors), and AD_44, 3,472 (1 donor), totaling 51,420 nuclei. In each panel, the full population is shown in light gray and the indicated group is overlaid, colored by inferred pseudotime (top), group identity (middle) or local nuclear density (2D kernel density estimate, bottom). Young nuclei occupy a discrete low-pseudotime region, whereas AD nuclei are shifted toward high pseudotime. b, Group-specific kernel density estimates of pseudotime, with the pooled distribution shown in gray. Nucleus and donor counts are as in a. Dashed vertical lines mark mean pseudotime: young 1.50, CTL 2.38, AD 2.90 and AD_44 2.12. The distribution shifts rightward from young to CTL to AD. c, Empirical cumulative distributions of nuclear pseudotime. The maximal vertical separation between AD and CTL is the Kolmogorov–Smirnov distance D = 0.27, presented as a descriptive effect size. Because nuclei within a donor are not independent, inference used donor-level mean pseudotime: AD versus CTL, 6 versus 7 donors, two-sided exact Wilcoxon rank-sum test, P = 0.0047. Young and AD_44 are shown descriptively and were not tested. d, Group composition of 22 fixed-width pseudotime bins (width 0.2, early to late from left to right). Each bar shows the fraction of nuclei contributed by each group. Nucleus and donor counts are as in a. Young and AD_44 were shown descriptively and were not tested. The AD fraction increases along pseudotime (Spearman ρ = 0.97, n = 22 bins, two-sided unadjusted P = 1.0 × 10−13), from near-absence in the earliest bins to dominance in the latest bins. A donor-aware binomial mixed model (in-segment versus out, group + (1 | donor), two-sided Wald tests, BH-adjusted across 44 segment × comparison tests) showed AD nuclei were underrepresented relative to CTL in early bins 4–9 (log-OR − 3.23 to −1.28, adjusted P ≤ 0.017) and overrepresented in late bins 16–21 (log-OR +0.62 to +1.31, adjusted P ≤ 0.044), with a single crossover at pseudotime ≈ 2.3–2.9. Exact estimates for every bin are in Supplementary Table 10. e, Nuclear pseudotime by group, with counts as in a. Center lines show medians, box bounds the 25th and 75th percentiles, and whiskers the most extreme observations within 1.5 × the interquartile range. Nuclei beyond the whiskers are plotted individually. This panel is descriptive. See c for donor-level inference. f, Top: per-nucleus expression of CSF1R, APOE, B2M and TIMP2 in microglia (same data as Fig. 4f). Violin widths show nuclear density. Embedded boxes show medians and 25th–75th percentiles, with whiskers extending to the most extreme observations within 1.5 × the interquartile range. Outliers are not drawn separately. Asterisks indicate FDRs from pseudobulk edgeR likelihood-ratio tests (AD versus CTL, 1 d.f., one pseudobulk per sample, 18 AD samples from 6 donors and 21 CTL samples from 7 donors, BH-adjusted across genes): CSF1R FDR = 3.1 × 10−7 (****). APOE, B2M and TIMP2 were nonsignificant (FDR ≥ 0.05). Young and AD_44 were shown descriptively and excluded from these tests. Bottom: CSF protein abundance in young healthy controls (<65 years, n = 38 participants), aged healthy controls (≥65 years, n = 167) and AD (n = 19). Center lines show medians, box bounds the 25th and 75th percentiles, and whiskers the most extreme observations within 1.5 × the interquartile range. Each dot represents one participant. g, Embeddings of microglial trajectory-associated genes, colored by trajectory rank (left) or correlation with AD status (right).

a, Concordance of AD-associated log2 fold changes between HypoAD (x-axis) and PsychAD dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (y-axis) for genes significant in both datasets (FDR < 0.05). Each point represents one gene. Black and pink indicate concordant and discordant directions, respectively. HypoAD differential expression used one pseudobulk per sample (18 AD samples from 6 donors, 21 control [CTL] samples from 7 donors). PsychAD used one pseudobulk per donor (AD/control donors: astrocytes 313/165, microglia 312/165, oligodendrocytes 312/165, OPCs 313/165, endothelial cells 305/159). Both analyses used edgeR likelihood-ratio tests. Two-sided, unadjusted Spearman correlations: astrocytes ρ = 0.656, n = 87 genes, P = 5.4 × 10−12. Microglia ρ = 0.588, n = 208, P = 9.7 × 10−21. Oligodendrocytes ρ = 0.894, n = 191, P = 1.2 × 10−67. OPCs ρ = 0.978, n = 17, P = 6.1 × 10−6. Endothelial cells ρ = −0.667, n = 8, P = 0.083. P values for OPCs and endothelial cells were computed exactly. The other three used the asymptotic t approximation because the exact algorithm underflowed. Dashed lines indicate zero. b, Age distribution of the 208 donors with microglia in the aging cohort. c, Homeostatic (blue), DAM1 (orange) and DAM2 (red) module scores versus age in the aging cohort (208 donors, 40,226 nuclei). Scores were averaged per donor and then per distinct age. Each point represents one of 64 age-level means. Lines show LOWESS fits (bandwidth 0.6). Spearman ρ and two-sided, unadjusted P values were computed across the 64 age-level means. d, Expression of homeostatic (CSF1R, CX3CR1, P2RY12), DAM1 (APOE, B2M, CTSB) and DAM2 (AXL, CLEC7A, TIMP2) markers in the aging cohort. Left: per-nucleus expression versus donor age, with LOWESS fits (bandwidth 0.5). Right: donors aged <65 years (149 donors, 31,118 nuclei) and ≥65 years (59 donors, 9,108 nuclei). Violin widths show nuclear density. Embedded boxes show medians and 25th–75th percentiles, with whiskers extending to the most extreme observations within 1.5 × the interquartile range. Asterisks indicate Benjamini–Hochberg (BH)-adjusted P values from donor-pseudobulk edgeR quasi-likelihood F-tests (≥65 versus <65 years, adjusted for sex, BH correction across all 34,176 genes): CX3CR1 3.0 × 10−3, P2RY12 1.7 × 10−2, APOE 3.3 × 10−8, B2M 1.8 × 10−4, AXL 1.1 × 10−2, CLEC7A 4.8 × 10−2. CSF1R (0.22), CTSB (0.26) and TIMP2 (0.51) were nonsignificant. *Adjusted P < 0.05, **adjusted P < 0.01, ***adjusted P < 0.001. Log2 fold changes and F statistics are in Supplementary Table 13. e, Age distribution of all 1,040 donors with microglia in the PsychAD AD cohort, including all diagnoses. Panels f and g use the 585 donors with a normal or AD diagnosis. f, Module scores as in c for the AD cohort (585 donors, 112,785 nuclei), computed across 59 age-level means. g, Expression as in d for the AD cohort: young controls (normal, <65 years, 95 donors, 18,764 nuclei), older controls (normal, ≥65 years, 165 donors, 28,330 nuclei), AD ≥ 65 years (312 donors, 63,760 nuclei) and early-onset AD (< 65 years, 13 donors, 1,931 nuclei). Asterisks indicate BH-adjusted P values from donor-pseudobulk edgeR likelihood-ratio tests (AD ≥ 65 versus older controls, 1 d.f., BH correction across all genes): APOE 6.7 × 10−6, CX3CR1 5.5 × 10−3, TIMP2 1.7 × 10−2. Other markers were nonsignificant. *Adjusted P < 0.05, **adjusted P < 0.01, ***adjusted P < 0.001. Log2 fold changes and likelihood-ratio statistics are in Supplementary Table 13.

a, Dot plot displaying the expression of key marker genes enriched in distinct hypothalamic subregions, as inferred by marker from their expression. Dot size represents the fraction of nuclei within a neuronal subtype expressing the gene; color intensity indicates the mean normalized expression level. b, UMAP of the top 30 neuronal subclusters with the highest number of DEGs. c, Strip plot showing log2FC values for significant DEGs identified across all 254 neuronal subtypes. Points are colored to indicate the predominant inferred hypothalamic subregion of the neuronal subtype in which the DEG is found. d, Inferred spatial localization of top AD-altered neuronal subtypes. Visium spots are colored by the predicted proportion of each indicated subtype, mapping transcriptional changes to anatomical space.

Inferred spatial localization of neuronal subtypes. Visium spots are colored by the predicted proportion of each indicated subtype, mapping transcriptional changes to anatomical space.

a, Dot plots showing maximum and mean log-normalized expression of neuropeptide genes and receptors across all hypothalamic neurons (213,469 nuclei from all young, CTL, AD and AD_44 donors). Error bars in mean-expression plots show the standard deviation across nuclei. This panel is descriptive. b, Concordance of AD-associated log2 fold changes between HypoAD (x-axis) and PsychAD dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (y-axis) in GABAergic (left) and glutamatergic (right) neurons. Each point represents a gene significant in both datasets (FDR < 0.05). For each gene and lineage, the result with the lowest FDR across constituent neuronal subtypes was selected. HypoAD differential expression used one pseudobulk per sample (AD versus CTL, edgeR likelihood-ratio tests), whereas PsychAD used one pseudobulk per donor. Two-sided, unadjusted Spearman correlations: GABAergic ρ = 0.028, n = 765 genes, P = 0.45. Glutamatergic ρ = 0.296, n = 301 genes, P = 1.7 × 10−7. Genes are correlation units, not biological replicates. Black and pink indicate concordant and discordant directions, respectively. Dashed lines indicate zero.

a, Ranked bar charts of univariate AUROC for distinguishing AD status using neuronal snRNA-seq pseudobulk PC1 scores (top) and MRI-derived volumetric measures (bottom). MRI participant counts are as in b. b, Cross-modal comparison of univariate AUROC between MRI-derived volume and neuronal snRNA-seq pseudobulk PC1 scores for matched hypothalamic regions (1:1 pairing). Left: snRNA-seq AUROC versus MRI AUROC, with a dashed line indicating equal performance. Right: AUROC estimates for each modality by region, with lines connecting matched estimates. Each dot represents one AUROC estimate, not a biological replicate. No error bars or cross-modal tests are shown. Score direction was chosen so that AUROC ≥ 0.5. The dashed vertical line indicates chance (AUROC = 0.5). MRI AUROCs used 316 participants: 24 with AD, defined as cognitively impaired and amyloid-β positive, and 292 without AD. snRNA-seq AUROCs used donor-level pseudobulks from 14 biologically independent donors (7 AD, 7 control) for ARC, PVH, SCN, MN, PO, TM, ZI and the whole hypothalamus, 13 donors (7 AD, 6 control) for LH, and 10 donors (5 AD, 5 control) for VMH and DMH. c, Cross-modal comparison as in b, with snRNA-seq AUROC averaged across neuronal subregion annotations containing the matched region. For example, AN includes ARC, ARC_SCN, ARC_SMN, LH_ARC, PO_ARC, SCN_ARC, VMH_ARC and ZI_ARC. Left: mean snRNA-seq AUROC versus MRI AUROC. Right: bars show MRI AUROC and mean snRNA-seq AUROC, and dots show individual annotation AUROCs. Error bars show sample standard deviations (n − 1 denominator) across annotations and appear only when at least three annotations match. Matching annotation counts are 8 (AN/ARC), 6 (Pa/PVH), 4 (VM/VMH), 10 (SCN), 2 (DM/DMH), 4 (MM/MN), 7 (MPO/PO), 1 (TM), 5 (ZI), 3 (LH) and 1 (whole hypothalamus). Standard deviations describe variation across annotations, not donor-level uncertainty. No inferential comparison was performed. All annotations originate from the same pool of 14 donors (7 AD, 7 control), so AUROCs averaged within a region are not statistically independent. MRI AUROCs and participant counts are as in b. AN and DM denote the arcuate nucleus and dorsomedial hypothalamic nucleus (ARC and DMH in the main text).

a, Schematic of the snRNA-seq workflow. Fresh whole hypothalamus was obtained from eight 8-month-old female mice: four wild-type (WT) and four 5xFAD heterozygous (HET). Tissue underwent Dounce homogenization, debris cleanup and nuclei isolation. Nuclei were loaded onto the 10x Chromium Controller, and 3′ gene-expression libraries were sequenced on a NovaSeq platform, yielding 60,479 nuclei for analysis. b, UMAP of 60,479 nuclei, colored by major cell type: astrocytes, endothelial cells, ependymal cells, microglia, leukocytes, neurons, oligodendrocytes, OPCs and fibroblasts. c, Cross-species cell-type correspondence. Heatmap of Spearman correlations between human HypoAD cell types (columns) and mouse 5xFAD cell types (rows), with mouse cell types labeled using transferred human annotations. High diagonal values indicate concordant cell-type identities across species. d, Microglial expression of homeostatic (Csf1r, Cx3cr1, P2ry12), DAM1 (Apoe, B2m, Ctsb) and DAM2 (Axl, Itgax, Timp2) markers in four WT mice (465 nuclei) and four HET mice (912 nuclei). Violin widths show nuclear density. Embedded boxes show medians and 25th–75th percentiles, with whiskers extending to the most extreme observations within 1.5 × the interquartile range. Outliers are not drawn separately. Arrows indicate the direction of change in HET. Genotype effects were estimated using linear mixed models of per-nucleus expression (genotype fixed effect, random intercept for mouse, lmerTest). Two-sided t-tests used Satterthwaite degrees of freedom, with Benjamini–Hochberg (BH) adjustment across nine genes. Genotype coefficients (HET − WT, 95% confidence interval) and adjusted P: Csf1r −0.36 (−0.73 to 0.01), 0.073. Cx3cr1 −0.33 (−0.60 to −0.06), 0.037. P2ry12 −0.37 (−0.65 to −0.09), 0.037. Apoe 0.62 (0.44 to 0.80), 1.3 × 10−4. B2m 0.06 (−0.08 to 0.21), 0.36. Ctsb 0.25 (0.06 to 0.43), 0.037. Axl 0.09 (0.03 to 0.16), 0.037. Itgax 0.06 (0.01 to 0.11), 0.037. Timp2 0.08 (−0.12 to 0.28), 0.37. ns, nonsignificant, *adjusted P < 0.05, ***adjusted P < 0.001. Pseudobulk edgeR results using mice as biological replicates are in Supplementary Table 16. e, Strip plot of log2 fold changes (5xFAD versus WT) for significant DEGs by cell type (pseudobulk edgeR likelihood-ratio tests, one pseudobulk per mouse, four WT and four HET mice, BH-adjusted FDR < 0.05). Each point represents one gene. Representative genes are labeled. f, Selected significantly enriched Hallmark pathways from GSEA of the 5xFAD-versus-WT comparison in astrocytes, neurons and oligodendrocytes. Fill color indicates the normalized enrichment score (NES). Gray indicates pathways not significantly enriched in that cell type. Illustrations in a created in BioRender; Yu, D. https://biorender.com/3747p8b (2026).

a, UMAP of the 5xFAD mouse dataset colored by predicted cell subtype, annotated by label transfer from HypoMap. The 66 predicted subtypes span glutamatergic (GLU), GABAergic (GABA), and non-neuronal populations, as listed in the legend. b, Selected significantly enriched Reactome pathways from GSEA of the 5xFAD-versus-WT comparison, shown for representative subtypes (02: Irx5.GLU-2, 04: Trh.GLU-2, 28: Mixed.GABA-2, 53: Etnppl.Astrocytes, 55: Ermn.Oligodendrocytes, and 57: OPC). Fill color indicates NES; gray indicates pathways not significantly enriched in that subtype. c, Strip plot showing log2 fold change (5xFAD versus WT) for significant DEGs across neuronal and non-neuronal subtypes. Each point is a gene; representative genes are labeled. d, UMAP of the 5xFAD mouse dataset colored by predicted hypothalamic subregion, annotated by label transfer from HypoMap (subregions listed in the legend). e, Selected significantly enriched Reactome pathways from GSEA of the 5xFAD-versus-WT comparison, aggregated by predicted subregion (arcuate nucleus, lateral hypothalamic area, medial preoptic area, non-neuronal, suprachiasmatic nucleus, and zona incerta). Fill color indicates NES; gray indicates pathways not significantly enriched in that subregion.

Newcastle United and Aston Villa are reportedly interested in signing Lille defender Nathan Ngoy, with several European heavyweights keeping tabs on the Belgian international ahead of a potential 2027 transfer battle.

The 23-year-old has enjoyed an impressive rise since joining Lille from Standard Liege in July 2025, establishing himself as an important figure in the French side’s defensive setup. His consistent performances have also earned him international recognition, making him an attractive proposition for several ambitious clubs.

According to a report from Fussball-News, AC Milan, Newcastle United, Aston Villa and PSG are closely monitoring the defender’s development, with the Italian giants potentially exploring a move as early as January.

The Premier League clubs, meanwhile, are believed to be considering a summer 2027 approach, while PSG are also keeping a close watch on his progress.

Aston Villa face major summer clear-out as six players approach potential exits

Lille are unlikely to sanction an inexpensive departure for one of their important defensive players. Ngoy remains under contract until the summer of 2029, putting the French club in a relatively strong negotiating position.

The report suggests Lille could demand about €40 million for his services, well above his current estimated market value of €25 million.

Ngoy has several qualities that make him an appealing target. Standing at 1.83 metres, the Belgian defender combines physical strength with impressive athleticism, positional awareness and composure when distributing the ball from the back.

His ability to contribute to the build-up could make him a particularly useful addition for clubs looking to improve their defensive options.

Want more CaughtOffside coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust.

Newcastle and Aston Villa could view Ngoy as a long-term defensive investment, while Milan are also looking to strengthen their backline.

However, Lille are unlikely to encourage a January departure, particularly with the defender remaining an important part of their plans.

Much will depend on whether the interested clubs are prepared to meet Lille’s financial demands. If Ngoy maintains his current level of performance, a competitive transfer battle could develop next summer.

Aston Villa could sanction major sale if £80m offer arrives

#1390. Thomas Frank announced as Crystal Palace boss as he eyes raid on Chelsea set-piece guru marginalised under Xabi Alonso

By BOBBY MANZI, FOOTBALL REPORTER and KIERAN GILL, MAIL SPORT REPORTER

Published: 10:07 EST, 16 November 2026 | Updated: 13:08 EST, 16 November 2026

Thomas Frank has been unveiled as Crystal Palace’s new manager on a two-and-a-half-year deal.

Frank has been out of work since being sacked by Tottenham Hotspur in February and has taken a significant pay cut to take over at Palace, who languish at the bottom of the Premier League.

However, he will earn more than his predecessor, Pierre Sage, who was sacked last week after winning just two of his ten league matches in charge.

New Palace boss Frank said: ‘It's an honour to sit here and be in charge of this fantastic Football Club. I'm really, really looking forward to it.

‘Crystal Palace is an iconic club in England and in the Premier League. I will do everything I possibly can to help and support the players and everyone around the place, and I'm really looking forward to meeting them.’

Across his spells at Brentford and Tottenham, Frank has managed 178 Premier League matches with a 34 per cent win rate.

Palace are set to approach Chelsea about Bernardo Cueva, who worked with Frank at Brentford before being poached to become the Blues' set-piece specialist.

We are pleased to confirm the appointment of Thomas Frank as Manager 🤝ℹ️ https://t.co/2wUzZAGt4S pic.twitter.com/zv2vMPGPFz

Palace are set to approach Chelsea about Cueva (right), who worked with Frank at Brentford

But Cueva may now be elevated back to the forefront of football if Palace can strike an agreement to bring him in to join Frank’s backroom staff. It is said Chelsea paid Brentford around £1million in compensation to hire him in 2024 at a time when his stock was high.

Cueva arrived at Chelsea in 2024. However, Daily Mail Sport revealed in the last summer how the 39-year-old Mexican’s role was changing after two seasons of work as Xabi Alonso’s side hired Austin MacPhee from Aston Villa as their new lead on set-plays.

Cueva has not been seen since then, either in training at Cobham or at matches at Stamford Bridge, but continued to work for Chelsea in more of an analytical role behind the scenes.

Club sources stressed at the time that it should not be seen as a demotion, and he is still listed on the first-team staff section of the website under the title ‘technical analyst’.

Chelsea are due to play Palace in two weeks' time at the Bridge on Wednesday, December 2.

Chelsea previously identified Cueva as a prime candidate for a role which had been vacant since Anthony Barry exited for Bayern Munich. Cueva, who also holds a UEFA Pro Licence through the Football Association, was regarded as an impressive acquisition in 2024.

Before joining Brentford in 2020 and helping them secure promotion to the Premier League, Cueva was at Chivas in his homeland of Mexico. He has also had a role with Norway men's national team.

#1389. Lethal Trent Alexander-Arnold sends Tuchel a statement in England victory

Thomas Tuchel has never been inclined to place much faith in the most famous right-back at his disposal, Trent Alexander-Arnold, once of Liverpool, now of Real Madrid, and – back in an England shirt – still capable of changing games in the blink of an eye.

England always looked likely to defeat a beleaguered Czech Republic team down to 10 men with just 25 minutes played, but it still required one man to conjure the moment of inspiration in this Nations League tie. This was the first cap in 15 months for the right-back now known simply as “Trent” in an England shirt – as well as his Real Madrid jersey – rather than the six syllables of his surname. With the game level at half-time, two minutes into the new half, he twice won the ball before landing a cross on the head of Anthony Gordon for the first goal.

TRENT ➡️ GORDON ⚽️🔥Anthony Gordon can't stop scoring for England, 3 goals in his last 3 games for England 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿#ITVFootball | @England pic.twitter.com/xmqPIULJ24

Will the Alexander-Arnold with England experiment survive? One feels that Tuchel will need a little more to convince him to abandon whatever reservations he has about the Liverpudlian. A week short of his 28th birthday, Alexander-Arnold was winning just his 35th cap. His Real Madrid team-mate Jude Bellingham, a second-half substitute, was earning his 58th cap less than two months after his 23rd birthday. Bellingham was on as captain in place of the man he replaced, Harry Kane, scorer of England’s second. Bellingham’s international career has taken a much less rocky path than that of his Real team-mate.

Having missed the World Cup finals this summer, and had little good fortune around previous tournaments, one wonders if Euro 2028 might be the watershed moment for Alexander-Arnold. Either way, against opponents who sit back, he is lethal when it is time for the big delivery. Alexander-Arnold may not have the breadth of England experience that some of his peers have accumulated, but he does have plenty of experience of big games.

“I make that run time and time again,” Gordon said of his anticipation of the Alexander-Arnold cross, “but only a set number of players have that ability, that technique and the bravery to risk a mistake to play that pass. And that’s why I have been dying to play with him [Alexander-Arnold]. He’s been on his own journey but has trained really well this week. He should have played more. Sorry – he would have loved to have played more.”

A Freudian slip from the Barcelona winger, another Liverpudlian in Spain, who himself has barely put a foot wrong for England of late. He has three goals in three games for England, including the World Cup semi-final against Argentina. This was an England team that Tuchel fine-tuned, first to give a rest to Bellingham and in other quarters, too. Lewis Hall started at left-back. Trevoh Chalobah won his third England cap at centre-back. Alex Scott, of Bournemouth, was given his debut off the bench in the second half and Rio Ngumoha won the second cap of his England career, just one month after his 18th birthday.

As for Kane, his 87th goal for England now puts him within two goals of Robert Lewandowski, among four greats in the seven ahead of Kane on the all-time international goalscorers’ list. By the end of this international break the England captain should have equalled Peter Shilton’s record 125 caps. It has been an astonishing career even if it ends tomorrow. Following the missed penalty against Spain, Kane was again the man in the right place at the right time when Morgan Rogers’s shot was blocked in the second half.

“Strange to get an early red card,” Tuchel said. “Not the best for the team and spectators. It’s an awkward one, but we kept going, got a win and that’s what counts.” Not quite a vintage Czech Republic team, either, and when their best player of the opening stages, the attacking midfielder Pavel Sulc, of Lyon in Ligue 1, was dismissed after 25 minutes, it certainly did not become any easier for the home team. Sulc, the Czech player of the year in 2025, had mistimed a tackle on Elliot Anderson, which on a VAR review, the Turkish referee Umut Meler decided was worthy of an upgrade from yellow to red. It was high on the right calf of the England midfielder.

Czech Republic DOWN TO 10 MEN! 🟥Pavel Šulc sees red for a dangerous challenge on Elliot Anderson#ITVFootball | @England pic.twitter.com/B2YOLuS0vL

England had looked once more a little open to the counter-attack in the early stages, with Sulc one notable runner. This was not an opponent of the quality of Spain and Tuchel’s players were able to recover the situation. When they lose the ball in the opposition’s half, England tend to look vulnerable.

Even before the red card Rogers had hit a post. Myles Lewis-Skelly, playing in midfield, was booked for a foul on Lukas Serv and was pursued thereafter by the Czech players hoping to get an upgrade on the yellow card. He was substituted at half-time, with Eberechi Eze on in his place.

“I spoke to Ant [Gordon] at half-time,” Alexander-Arnold said later to ITV, “and I said if I’m getting in those spaces make sure you get to the back post. You don’t expect to get it that fast, but it did and it worked.”

Two minutes after the break, Alexander-Arnold suddenly burst into life. He won the ball back in his own area and then drove forward in search of the return. When that did not come, he raced back to win the ball again and unleashed one of those right-footed outswingers to the back post, where Gordon guided in the header. “Really proud to score that,” Gordon said, “because I can’t tell you the number of hours I’ve spent practising headers.”

Kane scored the second just a minute before he was replaced and Bellingham took the captain’s armband and the role as a No 9. One day someone will have to step into those goalscorer’s boots on a permanent basis and try to replace Kane – although it may be a while yet.

Thomas Tuchel has backed Jude Bellingham as a future England captain after giving him the armband in the victory over the Czech Republic.

In the absence of Declan Rice, who was vice-captain at the World Cup, Bellingham assumed the role when he came on for Harry Kane, who is now in his 10th season as England captain and also scored in the 2-0 win in Prague.

Tuchel, who needs to check on Bellingham ahead of Saturday’s game against Croatia after a “niggle,” has praised the midfielder’s attitude during the extended international break one year after he was back from an injury but left out of the squad.

“If you are the captain at the end of these matches, you can be the permanent captain,” Tuchel said when asked whether Bellingham could eventually lead the team. “He was the captain against New Zealand before the World Cup. It is always a reward and always an honour.

“I think he loves to be with us at the moment. That’s what I feel, and we had this small talk today about his role. We felt in our hearts or our stomachs to say ‘let’s go again, let’s start again’ and also our heads told us maybe 30 minutes is enough for this match because he hasn’t played in this quick turnaround through this season. He has done it before, but not in the season, so we didn’t want to be the first ones to try that.

“But even in this little encounter, you can see that he’s confident and happy to help from the bench. So it’s a reward. It’s good. He had a little niggle at the end of the match, so hopefully it’s nothing serious, and he’s available for Croatia.”

Nico O’Reilly is a doubt for the Croatia match in Rijeka and there are also concerns over Ezri Konsa, who was on the bench but not fit enough to play.

Trent Alexander-Arnold provided an assist for Anthony Gordon in the Real Madrid full-back’s first cap in 15 months. Gordon, meanwhile, has now scored in the first two Nations League games of the campaign and is staking his case to be an indispensable player for Tuchel.

“He’s getting there. He’s defending his shirt, he’s defending his position, an excellent performance again after his performance against Spain,” Tuchel said.

“He was very decisive today and had an excellent goal. It was very, very difficult, but the technique and finishing was excellent. He scored against Spain, so he has decisive actions and he’s defending his shirt and his position. He does it on the highest level and he’s a very important player.”

England returned to winning ways with a 2-0 win over Czech Republic in Prague.

Pavel Sulc’s first-half red card after a VAR review of his clumsy challenge on Elliot Anderson took the sting out of the initially lively hosts and Anthony Gordon gave Thomas Tuchel’s men a deserved lead early in the second half.

The forward headed home a fantastic cross by Trent Alexander-Arnold, who was making his first start under the German coach, before skipper Harry Kane scored to settle any nerves.

So who played well for England and who failed to impress? Rate each player with our voting tool, and have your say in the comments.

I thought we were very professional second half. We stepped up and needed to be more dynamic, bring more urgency into our play, which we did. We kept that intensity going and and the effort was till there. Deserved victory.

Strange to get an early red card. Not the best for the spectators, not the best for the team. It’s an awkward one. But we got the win.

To guide it into the goal, there was an awful lot [for Anthony Gordon] to do. Good pass, good goal. Both full-backs were good. The position in the second half suited Trent more than the position in the first half. Lewis was excellent on the other side.

We have used all the outfield players after two matches so credit to all of them. Now it’s important to relax and enjoy the evening, do a good recovery and prepare for Saturday.

I think it was good. They go down to 10 men and it should be easier for us to win the game, But in fact it makes it more difficult. They get very compact and defend with a lot of players around the box and it’s hard to break them down.

We got that [goal] at the start of the second half which is what we needed. The longer it’s 0-0, it gets harder and harder and harder.

[Where do you place your assist?]  It’s up there for sure. I spoke to Ant at half-time and said if I get into those half-spaces I’m looking to put it in so make sure you get to the back post. I didn’t expect it to work so quickly.

He’s a willing runner, great to play with him. I saw the run and was able to execute the pass,

It’s always a pleasure and an honour to represent my country. It’s been a long time. I’ve always believed that I can play for England and I want to. The manager’s given me the opportunity and I tried to do what he wanted me to do to the best of my ability and I hope he’s happy with how I played.

🦁 #1301Alex Scott reflects on a special night, earning his first senior England cap 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿#ITVFootball | @gabrielclarke05 | @England pic.twitter.com/lC34bAPbbd

It was good, quite dominant. We created a lot of chances but without the quality. When they went a man down, we were too passive at times. We need to be dominant, as I said earlier, go for the throat and put teams away.

I said that to him [Trent, on the quality of the ‘assist’]. I make that run time and time again but only a set number of players have that ability, that technique and the bravery to risk a mistake to play that pass. And that’s why I have been dying to play with him. He’s been on his own journey but has trained really well this week. He should have played more. Sorry, he would have loved to have played more.

I’ve missed playing with Hally. He’s a good lad. We had great chemistry at Newcastle and it’s great to share this stage with him.

It’s my only header. I’d be the worst header of the ball you’ll ever see. Really happy, resally proud to score that because I can’t tell you the number of hours I’ve spent practising headers.

Perfectly competent and signs of promise in the left-back/left-wing axis. England looked too open against 11 men and better teams – hola España – may have capitalised on the sloppiness. But once Sulc was sent off, England gradually turned the screw and created a hatful of chances, running out easy winners.

Another tidy save from Kovar when Bellingham receives a pass from the left, strides towards the D, then drives a daisy-cutter towards the left of goal. The keeper swoops down early to turn it behind with a stiff wrist.

Two minutes of stoppage time are signalled as England try to pen the home side in their own half.

Tuchel has kept the back four on the pitch for the 90 minutes. He was not entirely happy with them in the first half – or his body language suggested that, anyway. But it is a welcomed clean sheet for England after the chaotic defeats to Spain and France.

Ngumoha is enjoying himself and showing off some excellent close control.

Scott and Eze smash shots over the bar from 22 yards within a minute of each other.

Rogers’ diagonal cross is chested down by Eze as he sets up an opportunity to shoot in the area but a defender hacks it away. Ngumoha pounces on the loose ball and plays a neat reverse pass with the outside of his boot to Rogers on the underlap. Rogers goes for power rather than lift to find Eze or Bellingham and the keeper makes another smart save.

Gibbs-White’s pace and direct running have the beating of Chaloupek and he tees up Eze to hammer a left-foot shot that seemed to be arrowing into the net until Kovar stuck up his right hand to paw it over.

Gordon stops, then from a standing start drives past bursts past Chaloupek to the byline and stands up a near-post cross that Rogers flashes wide.

Czech Republic break after England’s attack down the right hits the skids. Hlozek gallops down the middle and lets fly before Scott can catch him. Trafford sees it all the way, dives to his right to save and gathers the loopy effort from the rebound.

Slama hounds Ngumoha into conceding a corner as the Liverpool winger slips under pressure.

Jude Bellingham is wearing the England captain’s armband again. He was also wearing it during the pre-World Cup camp against New Zealand. Thomas Tuchel explained afterwards that the player with the most caps is skipper when Harry Kane is subbed off. Bellingham is also playing centrally, as a False Nine.

Bellingham → KaneNgumoha → SakaScott → Anderson.

England have switched to the Revie Plan with Bellingham as the deep-lying centre-forward.

Czech Republic 0 England 2 (Kane) Eze plays Rogers in down the left of the box. He gets there but falls under the tackle of Krejci, knocking the ball to Kane who thumps it through Hranac’s legs with his left foot from about seven yards.

KANE DOUBLES ENGLAND'S LEAD 🔥Harry Kane in the right place at the right time for the Three Lions 🦁#ITVFootball | @England pic.twitter.com/Od9x5kXOsH

Kane stuck around five finishes into that corner in the warm-up. Same finish - accurate and powerful. Finally a first cap for Alex Scott.

As Sam Matterface points out. England having a left-footed left-back has added an extra dimension to their attacking play. I never thought I’d be quoting Sam Matterface but it’s been one of those days. Ambros had taken up a good position in space on the left but the crossfield pass wasn’t good enough and sailed beyond him.

Alexander-Arnold shoots from the right after some slow-slow-slow-quick passing between him and Saka opens up a gap. But he drills it across goal and wide of the left post.

Now Hall does find the target at his third attempt this half but only because Krejci is there to deflect his cross on to the post with the keeper beaten.

Corner on the right for England who procrastinate so long over their positions the referee warns them but does not take it off them. Krejci and Kane have their arms around each other as the ball comes in and the Czech captain pulls Kane to the ground but the referee waves play on.

Saka takes it short and plays a one-two with Alexander-Arnold. Saka cuts it back to Eze to shoot in a pre-cooked move but he is closed down too quickly so he rolls it to Hall 20 yards out and the left-black leans back and launches his shot 20 rows back behind the goal.

England have a corner on the left after a last gasp tackle by Chaloupek on Gordon.

Czech Republic have switched to 3-3-3 in possession and are trying to play. Sadilek is struggling after being kicked by person or persons unknown. Apologies.

Although the goal was built from the right, England have been so dominant down the left. Hall and Gordon, who combined so well for Newcastle, do so again here with the left-back creeping up the inside while the winger goes down the outside and plays it into the box for his former colleague who wafts his shot wide with a lazy air from 15 yards. Should have scored.

Czech Republic 0 England 1 (Gordon) Alexander-Arnold clears Lingr’s cross and runs upfield to join the counter that seems to break down. But a crossfield pass from the home side is picked off by the right-back facing his own goal 30 yards from the Czechs’. He turns and arrows a fine cross to the left of the penalty spot. Gordon lets it bounce and cushions a header back across the keeper and in at the right post. Great finish. High IQ finish as he might say.

TRENT ➡️ GORDON ⚽️🔥Anthony Gordon can't stop scoring for England, 3️⃣ goals in his last 4️⃣ games for England 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿#ITVFootball | @England pic.twitter.com/iej0PCW8Ar

That goal was all about Trent. He intercepted in his own penalty area before making a 70-run up the pitch to get on the end of a throughball. That doesn’t work but he wins the ball back and crosses for Gordon to score. The full house from Trent there – showing Tuchel what he brings to the team in just a few seconds of action.

England are attcking from right to left in the second half. England’s trumpeter is in the house and reprises the national anthem.

Eze → Lewis-Skelly who was on a yellow card.

Just before half-time, Krejci, the Wolves centre-half wiped out Saka, watching the man, not the ball, and bodychecking him.

Thomas Tuchel was furious with the fourth official Cihan Aydin, wagging his finger in anger after Bukayo Saka was taken out by Ladislav Krejci. Before that he was quite passive on the touchline, hands in pockets as he watched England trying to break down the Czechs.

Could be another tactical half-time substitution for Myles Lewis-Skelly. Czech players definitely see him as the best chance of a red for England.

The Czech Republic were causing England problems with 11 men but having been reduced to 10 have concentrated on trying to persuade the referee to even up the numbers and also on defending in a low block. Gordon and Hall have the key to unlock the defence but too often when they have sent crosses in, Kane has been in wild rover mode.

Kane takes the ball by the left of the D, spins to wrap his right instep around the ball and try to bend it into the top right corner. Kovar, the PSV goalkeeper, soars to his left to claw it away with his top hand.

Kovář DENIS Harry Kane! 🛑England pushing for a goal before half time 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿#ITVFootball | @England pic.twitter.com/l4lAeAl6IE

Karabec is not going to be able to continue. Good cross from Hall from the left wins the applause of Kane. So near.

Karabec is hurt in a collision with Alexander-Arnold that the referee does not deem a foul.

Every tackle, every collision inspires a Czech demand for a red card. Karabec hits the deck like a bag of hammers when brushed by Rogers’ arm but the referee isn’t buying the implication that he had been elbowed.

Lewis-Skelly ignores Hall’s underlapping run down the inside left and pops it short to Guehi instead. The City defender slips a pass down the outside for Gordon who dribbles into the box and clips an inviting, low cross through the six-yard box. Rogers may have got a touch at the near post and the ball runs across goal. Karabec juts about gets it away,  avoiding the risk of shanking it into his own goal.

Krejci wants a tot-for-tat red card for Lewis-Skelly who slid in and caught Cerv on the foot. He never raised his studs and yellow suffices. The manager Santi is also booked for protesting the colour.

The system seems to be working again. Apologies for the break in updates.

Good work by Kane down the left to get away from Chaloupek and run into the box. He clips a short pass to the near post that Saka tries to finish, improvising a flick, that balloons wide off a defender. The angle made that all but impossible.

That is a big moment in the game, with Pavel Sulc dismissed for a stamp on Elliot Anderson. There was little protest about the foul when it occurred. In fact, even a yellow was a bit surprising. But Umut Meler was sent to the pitchside monitor. Czech Republic looked lively but you would now expect them to sit back and defend.

Czechs are now in a 5-4-0 formation. This will be a test of England to break through the two lines of defence. It will be like the Ghana match at the World Cup.

Pavel Sulc, who was playing so well, has been sent off after the referee was sent to the monitor by VAR. It was a high tackle, catching Anderson’scalf with his studs.

Czech Republic DOWN TO 10 MEN! 🟥Pavel Šulc sees red for a dangerous challenge on Elliot Anderson#ITVFootball | @England pic.twitter.com/B2YOLuS0vL

That red card has deprived the Czech Republic of their best player so far. He took it well rather than going off in a Sulc.

Big test for Czech manager Santi Denia, once of Atlético Madrid, who was manager of Spain U17s when they lost the 2017 final to an England team featuring – among other luminaries – Marc Guéhi and Morgan Gibbs-White.

Gordon cuts in from the left on to his right and flashes a shot across goal that flies past the right post.

SO CLOSE FROM GORDON!🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿#ITVFootball | @England pic.twitter.com/MUiKO8TqvC

Apologies we have been having some technical issues.

England had their best chance in the 16th minute when Rogers spun by the penalty spot. He was facing Anthony Gordon to collect his pass in from the left. Pirouetting, he steadies himself to thump a left-foot shot into the foot of the right post. The ball rebounds to Anderson who flays a shot from 18 yards that Chaloupek throws himself in front of to block only to divert it to Saka and Hranac is there to block that one.

How have England not scored!? 🤯Somehow Czech Republic keep the score at 0-0 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿 🇨🇿#ITVFootball | @England pic.twitter.com/51tmBwgRRf

England are dicing with danger in not picking up Sulc.

What was Thomas Tuchel saying about his England players being a danger to themselves around the box? It was an error there from Elliot Anderson that let Czech Republic through on goal and a better touch from Pavel Sulc would have seen them take the lead. Harry Kane dropped deep to start England’s attack down the right. The flanks will be their route to goal in this game.

Alexander-Arnold loses the ball in the middle of the park. Radosta is sent down the right by a cute pass and he gulls Hall by crossing early after shaping to go down the line. Alexander-Arnold is back to head it away but only as far as Cerv who torpedoes a volley from 25 yards barely a foot wide of the right post.

Kane is given a talking to for tangling with the Czech captain Krejci, giving him a deserved shove hopefully for the heinous crime of wearing the No 7 shirt while playing at centre-half.

Lewis-Skelly mops up at the back after a third rapid Czech Republic break, this one down the right with Chaloupek to the fore. Shielding the ball in the penalty area, he buys a foul and England build again from a free-kick.

The Professional Footballers’ Association has leapt to Cole Palmer’s defence following his withdrawal from the England squad.

“You see people like Cole Palmer, someone who would have played four consecutive summers in a row had he gone to the World Cup, and you wonder why is he missing?”He’s missing because he’s a victim of the calendar and that’s something that needs to absolutely trigger the alarm bells.”

He replaces Jarell Quansah in Thomas Tuchel’s line-up that lost to Spain at the weekend.

“Trent had a very good training week and the excellent training in Wembley after the match, where he showed that he absolutely wants to play and wants to be with us,” said Tuchel on the eve of the game at Fortuna Arena.

Trent Alexander-Arnold is in line to make his first England start under head coach Thomas Tuchel for tonight’s Nations League game against Czech Republic.

Injuries to Nico O’Reilly and Ezri Konsa have forced Tuchel into changes at the back, with Alexander-Arnold expected to come in at right-back, Trevoh Chalobah to replace Konsa and Lewis Hall to step in for O’Reilly.

Alexander-Arnold has made only one appearance under Tuchel, as a substitute in a World Cup qualifying win against Andorra in June 2025. His last start for England came under interim head coach Lee Carsley, when he scored in a victory over Finland.

Jude Belllingham could be given a rest after playing the full 90 minutes in the defeat by Spain, which would give Morgan Rogers an opportunity in the No 10 position.

Man City used ‘sham’ sponsorships in £830m cheating scheme

Manchester City arranged “sham” sponsorships in a near-£1bn plot to flout Premier League rules, an independent commission has found.

It was confirmed on Tuesday that City had been found guilty of all charges related to “serious breaches” of the league’s financial rules, with the commission also upholding all but one in relation to their failure to co-operate with an investigation spanning over three years.

The commission found that, of £949.94m City claimed in commercial income over a nine-year period, only £119.25m was legitimate, with the remaining £830.69m illicitly paid by their Abu Dhabi owners.

Good evening and welcome to live coverage of the Uefa Nations League match between Czech Republic and England from Slavia Prague’s Eden Stadium. The home side, 49th in the Fifa rankings, scrambled their way to World Cup qualification with victories in the play-offs in penalty shoot-outs over Ireland and Denmark, promptly stank Group A out in Mexico/Canada/United States, drawing with South Africa but losing to South Korea and Mexico to finish last.

Miroslav Koubek, their 74-year-old manager, the oldest in the competition’s history, promptly stood down and has been replaced by their first foreign head coach, Santi, the former Atlético Madrid centre-half, who spent 15 years moving from managing Spain’s U17s, to the U19s and then the U21s. Little wonder, given his CV, that he is looking to refresh his squad with a transfusion of young players, a requirement made all the more urgent by the international retirement of stalwart centre-forward Patrick Schick and the absence of West Ham’s Tomas Soucek who damaged his ankle in that 3-0 defeat by Mexico on June 25 and has not kicked a ball since.

Santi started his stint in charge and this campaign in Group A3 with a 2-1 defeat by Croatia but there were some very positive signs – they set up as a 4-3-3 in classic Spanish/Cruyff style and pressed like dervishes. England, who conceded three goals when players made mistakes when subjected to aggressive pressing in their opening 3-2 defeat by world champions Spain, will have to find better solutions tonight, either by holding their nerve or counterpressing with fewer mistakes.

Given England are ranked 45 places higher, their results, if not all performances, at the World Cup were commendable and the way in which they rattled Spain and should really have given themselves a bulwark against the comeback by converting their penalty at 2-1 up,  an away win should be relatively straightforward. But they did lose on their last visit to Prague in a Euro 2020 qualifier having won 5-0 in the home leg.

Arsenal and Manchester City are reportedly interested in signing RB Leipzig winger Antonio Nusa, with the Norwegian international attracting growing attention ahead of the January transfer window.

The highly-rated attacker could command a fee of up to £80 million.

La Gazzetta dello Sport reports that Milan are ready to enter talks with Club Brugge for Nicolò Tresoldi, knowing that the Belgian side will ask for €60m.

Milan have made U21 Germany international Tresoldi their top attacking target for the January transfer window, according to Gazzetta.

The pink paper already reported last week that Club Brugge’s asking price for Tresoldi in January will be €60m, and today’s update says the Rossoneri are ready to negotiate with the Belgians.

Whether they’ll eventually match that fee remains to be seen, but Tresoldi is surely the target the Serie A giants have identified to strengthen their attack.

Italy-born Tresoldi has represented Germany at youth levels and has scored 18 goals across all club and international competitions this season.

#1385. Man United hire private jet to get Mauricio Pochettino straight to Manchester after final USA game in Cincinnati - and new boss is expected to start work as soon as he steps off the plane!

Published: 11:27 EST, 16 November 2026 | Updated: 13:55 EST, 16 November 2026

Manchester United have laid on a private jet for Mauricio Pochettino to fly straight to England in the early hours of Wednesday morning after he finishes work as US national team coach.

Pochettino’s last game in charge is against Haiti in Cincinnati, which kicks off at midnight on Tuesday UK time. The 54-year-old will speak to the media and say farewell to his players before jumping on a plane to Manchester which has been organised by United.

It will enable Pochettino to sleep before he lands in the UK on Wednesday morning ready to go straight to Carrington and start work.

He will be accompanied by first-team coach Miguel D’Agostino, strength and conditioning coach Silvia Tuya and analyst Alec Scott.

It has emerged that three other members of his trusted coaching team – assistant Jesus Perez, goalkeeper coach Toni Jimenez and his son and fitness coach Sebastiano Pochettino – were allowed to travel to Manchester at the weekend after the US won the first leg against Haiti 6-0 in Miami.

It means that Pochettino’s back-room staff have been able to make a headstart in their preparations for his first game in charge against Liverpool at Anfield on Sunday. It is a huge fixture in the calendar for United, but even more so because he takes over a team languishing in the relegation zone.

Man United have laid on a private jet for Mauricio Pochettino to fly straight to England after he finishes work as US national team coach

Pochettino will take charge of his final match as USA boss in Cincinnati before boarding the direct flight to Manchester

Pochettino's long-time assistant Jesus Perez is one of three trusted staff members who have already been given permission to travel to Manchester

Pochettino will be able to work with the players as they begin reporting back from international duty, and is expected to speak to club media before conducting his pre-match press conference on Friday lunchtime.

Speaking ahead of the second leg against Haiti at the TQL Stadium, Pochettino said: ‘I am with Miguel, Sylvia and Alec and after they are going to join me in Manchester.

‘The next question is where are Jesus, Toni and Sebastiano? They are ahead. After the game (in Miami), they flew to Manchester and they are there in advance. That was the plan when we agreed terms with Manchester United and with the US national team.

‘They are there preparing everything because on Wednesday, when we arrive, it’s going to be non-stop and then we start with playing games.’
