For each group of environmental variables, principal components were calculated and selected until the cumulative explained variance reached 80%; these components were used as predictors in the GDM. Colour shading denotes individual principal component dimensions. Variable loadings are shown in Extended Data Fig. 7. Model statistics and predictor importance using Monte Carlo sampling with 250 permutations are reported in Supplementary Tables 2 and 3. Landscape context is represented by the mean forest cover within a 200 m concentric buffer surrounding each plot.

The three taxonomic groups with the strongest explanatory power—understorey plants, fungi and bacteria—also exhibited homogenization in the agricultural land uses (Fig. 2). This pattern suggests that homogenization is driven, to a large extent, by deterministic processes associated with land-use-induced changes in the environment, including direct impacts from soil disturbance and fertilization, and indirect effects from the deliberate replacement of forest species with a single, often non-native, target crop, and an alteration of vegetation structure by establishing even-aged structure. Additionally, biotic homogenization is driven by characteristics of the surrounding landscape (Supplementary Table 3). Processes leading to biotic differentiation can also emerge from changes in vegetation structure, as observed in most canopy-dwelling groups. Thus, for many groups, homogenization and differentiation can be linked to drastic changes in habitat structure following land-use intensification30 and in the remaining surrounding forests. Still, biotic differentiation can also be only weakly related to environmental conditions and the surrounding landscape, as for leaf litter spiders, mesostigmatid mites and springtails. Thus, biotic differentiation could be more stochastic and potentially driven by disturbance, legacy effects or meta-population and meta-community dynamics that were not quantified here.

Our results provide detailed insights into how tropical land-use intensification restructures biodiversity through concurrent changes in species richness and community composition. We document pronounced declines in γ- and α-multidiversity from lowland forests to monocultures, driven primarily by aboveground taxa. The diminishing tropical (degraded) forests and traditional agroforestry systems in our study region constitute irreplaceable reservoirs of biodiversity, but their biodiversity is in peril and requires urgent conservation and restoration actions. Divergent responses between aboveground and belowground compartments underscore the need to integrate multiple taxonomic groups spanning body size and mobility. We found no evidence for consistent community homogenization with land-use intensification. Instead, consistent with previous work, we found taxon-specific and seemingly idiosyncratic patterns of both biotic homogenization and differentiation19,20,22,50, but we also revealed a systematic shift from turnover to nestedness in monocultures. Our results call for careful interpretation of spatial patterns of community homogenization and differentiation, as well as long-term monitoring, because homogenization–differentiation trends can be scale-dependent (in line with the landscape divergence hypothesis) and can differ between smallholder and industrial plantations, which are not included in our study. In addition, early stages of assemblage simplification may mask trajectories towards biotic homogenization. Overall, our results demonstrate that land-use intensification alters multidiversity across spatial scales, with ecosystem-wide consequences for biotic communities and their abiotic environment, and suggest that habitat filtering has a stronger role than neutral or dispersal processes. Effective conservation will benefit from recognizing the conservation value of traditional agricultural systems, which, in our study region, buffer the loss of multiple generalist forest species and exhibit high levels of β-diversity. These traditional agricultural systems are currently under pressure from conversion and lie outside the conservation focus and landscape planning. Furthermore, implementing sustainable management practices2,3,4 within conventional monocultures could help mitigate biodiversity losses and promote landscape differentiation in these agricultural landscapes. Differentiation across multiple taxonomic groups should not overshadow the homogenization occurring within key taxonomic groups such as bats, birds, trees and understorey plants. Therefore, there is a growing need to establish conservation priorities for focal taxonomic groups, including tailored landscape-scale solutions to maximize the γ-diversity of forest-associated biodiversity, such as conserving irreplaceable endemic species in this biodiversity hotspot.

Our study was conducted in the province of Jambi on the island of Sumatra, Indonesia. This tropical lowland region has undergone extensive land-use changes since the twentieth century and is a showcase of smallholder agriculture in Indonesia13,42. Two sample landscapes, ‘Harapan’ and ‘Bukit Duabelas’ (with loam and clay Acrisol soils, respectively), were selected within Jambi Province. In each landscape, four 50 m × 50 m replicate plots were established in each of the four land-use types common to the region: primary degraded forest (sensu ref. 51), jungle rubber (a traditional agroforestry system established by planting rubber trees inside secondary forest), smallholder monoculture rubber plantation, and smallholder monoculture oil palm plantation—totalling 32 plots. The number of replicate sites per land use is comparable to that of other ecological studies in tropical lowland regions52. Various measurements, such as microclimate, were taken at the plot level. Other measurements, such as most biodiversity sampling, were taken in five permanent 5 m × 5 m subplots established within each plot. All sites were selected in 2012. At this time, rubber plantations were established 7–16 years ago, and oil palm plantations were established 8–15 years ago. For jungle rubber, plots selected contained older non-rubber trees, with individual rubber trees of varying ages not planted in rows13.

Jungle rubber, rubber and oil palm plots were owned and managed by smallholder farmers, whereas the forest plots were located in the Bukit Duabelas National Park and the Harapan Rainforest Restoration concession area (PT REKI). In our study region, smallholders generally do not cultivate food crops alongside the target cash crops examined here, with only a few exceptions8,42,43. Our study’s oil palm plots were on average surrounded by ~13.6% forest and ~61% oil palm plantations within 1 km buffers compared with ~0.45% and ~96% in industrial oil palm plantations, respectively41. Further, our oil palm plots received less herbicide (0.73 l ha−1 year−1) and fertilizer (6.6 kg N ha−1 year−1) compared with industrial oil palm plantations41 (1.12 l ha−1 year−1 and 141 kg N ha−1 year−1). Rubber and oil palm smallholder plantations represent the highest land-use intensity level among the systems included in our study. Yet land-use intensity is even higher in large-scale industrial plantations. More information on the study region, study design, land-use types and management practices of the smallholder systems is provided elsewhere8,13,42. Data compilation in these studies has also served as a basis for our study, but has been substantially expanded in recent years. For example, a multi-taxon perspective was offered in ref. 42 for 3 taxonomic groups, in ref. 13 for 9 taxonomic groups, and in ref. 8 for 14 taxonomic groups.

We studied 24 different biodiversity indicators distributed from the canopy to the soil, namely: (1) ants (Hymenoptera: Formicidae), (2) beetles (Coleoptera), (3) true bugs (Hemiptera), (4) flies (Diptera)53, (5) parasitoids (parasitoid Hymenoptera), (6) spiders (Araneae), and (7) springtails (Collembola), from the canopy; (8) bats (Chiroptera), (9) birds (Aves), (10) butterflies (Lepidoptera), (11) trees (Tracheophyta), (12) understorey plants (Tracheophyta), (13) spiders, (14) beetles, and (15) ants, from the leaf litter; (16) centipedes (Chilopoda), (17) springtails, (18) mesostigmatid mites (Mesostigmata), and (19) oribatid mites (Oribatida), from the litter and soil; and (20) fungi, (21) testate amoebae, (22) protists, (23) bacteria, and (24) archaea, from the soil (Supplementary Table 4). These biodiversity indicators represent a wide spectrum of taxa, encompassing all domains of life, various trophic levels, and diverse ecological strategies, dispersal abilities and body sizes. This comprehensive dataset builds on a long-term collaborative effort that generated detailed insights into individual taxonomic groups, including species descriptions54,55,56,57,58,59, field guides60,61,62,63 and functional and trophic interactions53,64,65,66—as well as ecosystem-wide analyses and integrative studies linking ecological and socio-economic dimensions8,13,42.

Canopy arthropods (ants, beetles, bugs, flies, parasitoids, spiders and springtails) were collected by canopy fogging in the dry season from May to October 2013. In each of the 32 plots, 3 representative canopy locations were selected, avoiding canopy gaps and overly dense canopies. At each of the 3 locations, 16 rectangular traps (1 m × 1 m) fitted with 100 ml ethanol-filled bottles were suspended from ropes beneath the selected canopies at approximately 1.50 m. 50 ml of DECIS EC 25 (active ingredient: deltamethrine 25 g l−1), dissolved in 4 l of petroleum white oil, was applied to the target canopies from the ground using the Swingtec Swingfog SN 50. In all four land-use systems, target canopies consisted of leaves from different trees. Stunned and dead arthropods were collected from the traps up to 2 h after the complete application of the fogging mixture. Canopy fogging was conducted in the early morning, immediately after sunrise, to minimize air movement that would disperse the fog. This was done only in dry conditions, ensuring that small arthropods would not become trapped in water droplets on leaves and branches. Overall, 372,146 canopy arthropod individuals were collected this way53 and sorted into morphospecies for selected taxa. This study includes data from the following taxa: ants (Hymenoptera: Formicidae) 179 morphospecies67; beetles (Coleoptera) 397 morphospecies in 4 families (Chrysomelidae, Curculionidae, Elateridae and Staphylinidae)68; true bugs (Hemiptera) 301 morphospecies in 2 suborders (Auchenorrhyncha and Heteroptera); flies (Diptera) 483 morphospecies in 2 suborders (Brachycera and Nematocera, including Eudiptera)69; parasitoid wasps (Hymenoptera: “Parasitica”) 1,012 morphospecies in 6 families (Braconidae, Ceraphronidae, Encyrtidae, Eulophidae, Scelionidae and Platygastridae)70; spiders (Araneae) 445 morphospecies71; and springtails (Collembola) 60 morphospecies72. Recorded (morpho-)species across taxa are deposited in the http://ecotaxonomy.org database and in refs. 60,61,62.

Bats were surveyed using mist nets and harp traps between April and August 2015. We used telescopic aluminium poles to install mist nets with a total length of 48 m, as well as two harp traps (1.35 m × 1.75 m) in presumed bat flyways. Mist nets were 3 m high, with a 19-mm mesh size, and were installed at ground level or up to 3 m high, depending on plot conditions. Each plot was sampled from 17:30 to 22:00 on two consecutive nights, resulting in an average sampling effort of 1,296 m2 of mist net hours. We checked the nets and traps every 15 min until 20:00 and every 30 min thereafter. Harp traps were left on site until and checked the morning after. Captured bats were left in tissue pouches until the nets were closed. Then bat morphology was measured to identify them according to the latest bat species checklist for Sumatra73. We tagged the bats’ nails with nail polish colour codes to identify recaptures and released them afterwards. This study includes data from 20 bat species. In plot HJ3, no individuals were caught (total abundance = 0).

Birds were sampled with point counts74, as well as automated sound recordings, from May to July 2013. Point counts and automated sound recordings lasted 20 min and were conducted from the centre of each plot between 6:00 and 10:00. The timing of point counts alternated between early and late morning, and all plots were visited three times. The automated sound recorders (SM2+ with two SMX-II microphones, Wildlife Acoustics) were set up at ~2 m height to record at a 44.1 kHz sampling rate in stereo, simultaneously across land-use types; one recording, starting at sunrise, was used for each plot. Point count detections of individuals flying above the canopy were excluded, and unfamiliar bird calls were recorded using a Sennheiser ME-66 directional microphone. The automated sound recordings were uploaded to ecoSound-web, an online platform for ecoacoustics75, for two independent ornithologists to identify all bird calls within an estimated 35 m radius. Only bird species identified by both ornithologists in recordings of each plot were used and subsequently merged with the species list obtained from the point counts. Aural detections were confirmed with cross-checks on the Xeno-Canto online bird call database (https://xeno-canto.org/). This study encompasses data from 114 bird species. For birds, BO1_5 data were unavailable. Therefore, when analyses required non-missing values, imputation was performed by using the average from plots of the same land use within the same landscape (that is, Bukit). However, γ-diversity values for birds may be underestimated.

Butterflies (Lepidoptera: Papilionidae, Pieridae, Lycaneidae and Nymphalidae) were recorded from all 32 study plots in the dry season of 2017 between August and October. Butterflies were collected using sweep netting on three parallel 50-m transects per plot, with two transects on the outer boundaries and the third through the centre. Sweep netting was conducted once in the morning (8:00−11:00) and repeated in the afternoon (13:00−16:00). Except for two voucher specimens per collected species, all butterfly individuals were released on the evening of the sampling day. This study includes data based on butterfly specimens from 219 species76. Recorded morphospecies are deposited in the http://ecotaxonomy.org database and in ref. 63.

Plant inventories were conducted between February 2013 and August 2014, using different sampling schemes for large trees and vascular understorey plants30. All trees per plot with a diameter of ≥10 cm at a height of 1.3 m were identified. Vascular understorey plants were censused in the five 5 m × 5 m subplots per plot, including all plant individuals, such as terrestrial plants (herbs, shrubs, climbers and juvenile trees) and epiphytes growing up to 3 m above the ground. 281 tree species were present in both censuses (for large trees and understorey plants). To avoid inflating species richness, they were retained only in the matrix that included large trees. Species identification was conducted in the field if possible or otherwise based on field photographs and herbarium specimens deposited at BIOT, BO, GOET, and the herbaria at Jambi University and Harapan Rainforest (acronyms follow Index Herbarium: http://sweetgum.nybg.org/science/ih/). The number of all individuals per species and plot was used for analyses. In total, this study includes 443 tree species and 976 vascular plant species in the understorey.

Leaf litter was collected from three of the five subplots within each of the study plots. In each subplot, leaf litter from 1 m2 of ground was sieved using a coarse mesh (width of 2 cm). All macro-invertebrates visible to the naked eye were hand-collected from the sieved samples, stored in 65% ethanol and transported to the laboratory for identification12. Recorded (morpho-)species are deposited in the http://ecotaxonomy.org database. This study includes data on 135 morphospecies of ants, 170 morphospecies of beetles, and spider specimens from 132 morphospecies. For leaf litter spiders and leaf litter beetles, no individuals were detected in plots HO2 and BO4, respectively (total abundance = 0).

Between October and November 2013, random samples were taken from three 5 m × 5 m subplots per plot (a total of 96 samples). Samples were taken at least 2 m from the next tree or dead-wood accumulation. Each sample measured 16 cm × 16 cm and included the complete litter layer and the underlying topsoil to a depth of 5 cm, obtained using a spade. Animals were extracted using heat and stored in 70% ethanol77. This study includes data from 12 morphospecies. In plot BR2, no individuals were detected (total abundance = 0).

Samples were taken in October 2013. In each plot, one randomly positioned soil core (16 cm × 16 cm) was taken to a depth of 5 cm in the mineral soil. Litter and soil layers were separated in the field and extracted independently. Animals were extracted by heat for 5–10 days until the substrate was completely dry78, collected in dimethyleneglycol–water solution (1:1) and stored in 70% ethanol79. This study includes data from 58 morphospecies.

Three soil cores were taken in October and November 2013 from each of 32 plots. Soil cores (16 cm × 16 cm) were collected from the litter layer and the underlying soil to a depth of 5 cm. Animals were extracted under a heat gradient78, collected in dimethyleneglycol–water solution (1:1) and thereafter stored in 70% ethanol. Identification of soil mites was done on microscopic slides to (morpho)species level. Recorded (morpho)species are deposited in the http://ecotaxonomy.org database. More details are described in ref. 80. This study includes data from 110 morphospecies of mesostigmatid mites and 219 morphospecies of oribatid mites.

Soil samples were collected in October and November 2016. In three subplots (5 m × 5 m) per plot, five soil cores (15 cm depth, 4 cm diameter) were taken and pooled, yielding a total of three samples per plot. Samples were sieved (50 × 50 mm mesh) and freeze-dried. DNA extraction, sequencing, and assignment of OTUs have been described81. Data have been deposited in the Dryad repository82. This study includes data from 12,309 OTUs.

Litter and upper mineral soil samples (to a depth of 50 mm) were collected in October and November 2013 using a 50 mm diameter corer. Testate amoebae were extracted from the samples by washing 1 g dry weight sample through a 500-µm mesh and back-sieving the filtrate through a 10-µm mesh. More details are described in ref. 83. This study includes data from 190 morphospecies of testate amoebae.

Soil samples were collected from each study plot and processed (sieving, freeze-drying and milling) to extract DNA for protist community analysis84. This study includes data from 5,204 OTUs of protists.

Soil samples were taken at the subplot level, DNA was extracted and amplicons were generated with primer pairs targeting the 16S ribosomal RNA gene of bacteria and archaea and used to assess bacterial and archaeal community compositions separately33. This study includes data on 16,413 bacterial OTUs and 448 archaeal amplicon sequence variants. For archaea, HF3 data were unavailable. Therefore, when analyses required non-missing values, imputation was performed by using the average from plots with the same land use within the same landscape (that is, Harapan). However, γ-diversity values for archaea may be underestimated.

We consider 24 environmental variables distributed into 4 groups: microclimate, vegetation, litter and soil (Supplementary Table 5).

Meteorological stations were set up in the centre of each plot to measure hourly below-canopy air temperature and relative humidity at 2 m height between June 2013 and October 2014. Additionally, soil sensors were used to measure soil temperature and moisture at a depth of 0.3 m (ref. 85).

Different aspects of structural complexity have been measured using terrestrial laser scanning in each of the 32 plots in September and October 2016. Based on a single-scan approach, we calculated the effective number of layers, which quantifies vertical stratification86, and the stand structural complexity index87, which describes the complexity of vegetation’s three-dimensional occupation of space. We collected nine single scans, evenly distributed across each plot, and aggregated at the plot level using mean and standard deviation, the latter describing the spatial heterogeneity of vegetation structure88. Additionally, hemispherical photographs were taken at 1.2 m above the ground from 32 positions within each plot to derive canopy openness42. Fine root production was estimated by installing 16 ingrowth cores per plot8.

Aboveground litterfall was assessed by placing 16 litter traps (75 cm × 75 cm) in each plot. Traps were emptied monthly from March 2013 to April 2014. For oil palms, pruned leaves were counted, and a subsample was dried and weighed. For litter nutrients, aliquots of material from the litter–fermentation layer of all 32 plots were dried at 65 °C for 72 h, milled, and analysed for total C and N concentrations using an elemental analyser89 (Carlo Erba Instruments).

Soil sampling was conducted in 2013. Within a 50 m × 50 m area at each site, ten grid points were selected (including the five subplots), and soil samples were taken from the top 0–0.1 m depth. The ten subplots were averaged to represent each site. Soil biochemical characteristics (that is, pH, soil organic carbon (kg C m−2), total nitrogen (g N m−2), 15N natural abundance signatures (‰ 15N), effective cation exchange capacity (ECEC; mmolc m−2), base saturation (%), aluminium saturation (%) and extractable phosphorus (g P m−2)) were determined on air-dried and sieved (2 mm) soil samples. Organic carbon and total nitrogen were analysed using a CN analyser (Vario EL Cube, Elementar Analysis Systems) and 15N by isotope ratio mass spectrometry (Delta Plus, Finnigan MAT). ECEC was determined by percolating the soils with unbuffered 1 mol l−1 NH4Cl, and cations (Ca, Mg, K, Na, Al, Fe and Mn) were measured in percolates using an inductively coupled plasma-atomic emission spectrometer (iCAP 6300 Duo VIEW ICP Spectrometer, Thermo Fisher Scientific). Base and aluminium saturation were calculated as percentage exchangeable bases or aluminium on the ECEC. Extractable phosphorus was determined using the Bray 2 method for acidic tropical soils. Soil physical characteristics for each site included bulk density (g cm−3; core method)32,90. Soil respiration was measured monthly in 2013 using a chamber located on four subplots per plot. Gas samples were analysed using a gas chromatograph with an electron capture detector and a flame ionization detector (GC 6000 Vega Series2, Carlo Erba Instruments)91.

Species matrices. Species observations taken at the subplot level were aggregated into plot-level observations.

Environmental data. We conducted a principal component analysis for each group of variables, with variables transformed (when needed) and scaled. We selected the first components until the cumulative explained variance reached 80%. Variable contributions of these selected principal components are displayed in Extended Data Fig. 7.

Landscape data. We calculated landscape metrics within 200 m buffers around our plot centres using a manually classified land-use map derived from satellite imagery from 2016 (ref. 92). We used the R package landscapemetrics93 to calculate the mean forest coverage.

Species occurrences were calculated separately for each taxonomic group.

α- and γ-diversities. We quantified diversity using the Hill number framework, expressing it as effective species numbers, where q0 disregards species abundances and is therefore more sensitive to rare species (species richness) and q1 weights species in proportion to their abundances, favouring neither rare nor dominant species (that is, effective number of common species; Shannon diversity)94. In addition, we calculated rarefaction–extrapolation curves for the 24 taxonomy groups at plot (that is, α-diversity; Supplementary Figs. 1 and 2) and each land use (that is, γ-diversity; Supplementary Fig. 3) level using the iNEXT R package95,96.

α- and γ-multidiversity. To assess the multidiversity across all 24 taxonomic groups, first, we normalized the observed effective number of species at the plot or land-use type level using the min–max scaling approach, following: y = (x − min(x))/(max(x) − min(x)), where x is the set of observed effective number of species. The normalized effective number of species (y) ranges between 0 and 1, with 0 referring to the lowest observed value and 1 to the highest observed value for each taxonomic group across plots or land uses. This method ensures equal weight for all taxonomic groups, despite differences in their diversity ranges, and is a common approach in multi-taxon studies1,97. To obtain a single α-diversity index, we averaged the normalized values—that is, the overall diversity across all taxonomic groups at the plot level (α-multidiversity). For γ-multidiversity, we likewise averaged the normalized values—that is, based on the lowest and highest observed diversity values at the land-use types. In addition, we calculated α- and γ-multidiversity separately for aboveground and belowground taxonomy groups.

β-Diversity and β-multidiversity. For each taxonomic group, we calculated β-diversity using pairwise dissimilarity matrices (presence–absence data; index family = jaccard; Supplementary Fig. 7). The Jaccard pairwise dissimilarity (βjacc, total β-diversity) among plots was computed as βjacc = βjtu + βjne, where βjtu accounted for turnover and βjne accounted for the nestedness (measured as the nestedness-resultant dissimilarity fraction of Jaccard dissimilarity), measured on a normalized scale from 0 to 1. Calculations were performed using the beta.pair from the package betapart v1.6. Mathematically, in cases of complete biodiversity loss—that is, zero individuals detected—plots have a total β-diversity of one as they do not share species with other plots; in these cases, we assumed turnover to be 0 and nestedness to be 1, considering that β-diversity result from species losses; this was implemented manually as it is not included in the output of betapart98,99. We also calculated β-diversity using Sørensen and its components and the abundance-based indices Bray–Curtis (weights absolute differences in abundance equally, so that abundant species contribute most to dissimilatiry)100 and Morisita–Horn (weighted towards common and dominant species and it is robust to sample size)101. These abundance-based dissimilarity indices were calculated using the vegan R package102 (Bray–Curtis: method = “bray”, binary = F; and Morisita–Horn dissimilarity: method = “horn”, binary = F; Supplementary Fig. 8). For Morisita–Horn, it is not possible to calculate dissimilarity when communities have zero abundance. Therefore, for Morisita–Horn, plots with at least one taxon for which the abundance was zero were excluded (BO4, BR2, HJ3, HO2 and HR4). We aggregated the pairwise dissimilarities to a mean pairwise dissimilarity for each taxonomic group for each plot (n = 32 plots for 24 taxonomic groups). To calculate β-multidiversity, we normalized the aggregated pairwise dissimilarity at the plot level using the min–max scaling approach1,97, as y = (x − min(x))/(max(x) − min(x)), where x is the set of pairwise dissimilarity at plot level. The normalized pairwise dissimilarity (y) ranges between 0 and 1, with 0 referring to the lowest observed value and 1 to the highest observed value for each taxonomic group across plots. We average the normalized β-diversity values across taxonomic groups at the plot level (either including all taxonomic groups or only aboveground and belowground taxonomic groups).

We used the ANOVA type II test to assess the influence of land use on α- and β-multidiversity. In addition, we used ANOVA type III to evaluate the influence of land use, compartment (aboveground and belowground), and their interaction. This analysis was implemented in the car package103. We checked for normality and homogeneity of variance of residuals using the Shapiro–Wilk test and Levene’s test for homogeneity of variance. Further, we tested statistical pairwise differences using multiple comparisons of means with Tukey, with P values adjusted with the false discovery rate—that is, the expected proportion of false discoveries amongst the rejected hypotheses104—using the p.adjust function (fdr) in the stats R package.

For each taxon, we determined significant differences in diversity (α or β) of the current land use compared with the forest by calculating log ratio and 95% adjusted bootstrap confidence intervals as follows:

where ‘agricultural land use’ is the diversity value in the agricultural land use and ‘\(\overline{\mathrm{forest}}\)’ is the mean of the diversity in the forest. Negative and positive values indicate decreases and increases in diversity compared to the forest, respectively. For α-diversity, a pseudocount of 1 was added to all species count values to handle zeros while symmetrically preserving relative differences for count-like data—that is, \(\log [({\rm{a}}{\rm{g}}{\rm{r}}{\rm{i}}{\rm{c}}{\rm{u}}{\rm{l}}{\rm{t}}{\rm{u}}{\rm{r}}{\rm{a}}{\rm{l}}\,{\rm{l}}{\rm{a}}{\rm{n}}{\rm{d}}\,{\rm{u}}{\rm{s}}{\rm{e}}+1)/(\bar{{\rm{f}}{\rm{o}}{\rm{r}}{\rm{e}}{\rm{s}}{\rm{t}}}+1)]\). In the case of turnover and nestedness (0–1-scaled data), zeros were handled by adding 50% of the minimum non-zero value prior to log ratio calculation105, specifically, a pseudocount of 0.0357 was added for turnover (minimum non-zero value = 0.0714) and 0.00256 was added for nestedness (minimum non-zero value = 0.0051). We then calculated 95% confidence intervals for the log ratio using 10,000 bootstrap replicates (R package boot106, adjusted percentile bootstrap (bca-type)). If the 95% confidence intervals did not include zero, this indicated a significant difference between land use and the forest. As the results for diversity changes were largely consistent across q0 and q1 (Supplementary Fig. 9), we only show the results for q0. In addition, we performed t-tests to assess for significant differences between the log ratio and zero (forests as a reference), adjusting the P values using the false discovery rate (Supplementary Results).

We calculated Pearson’s correlation with false discovery rate correction for species richness and pairwise Jaccard dissimilarity indices between each taxonomic group, irrespective of land-use type. The correlations are displayed in Supplementary Fig. 5.

Dissimilarities between pairwise observations were calculated separately for each taxonomic group and land use. Pairwise Jaccard dissimilarity was calculated using vegdist function (method = jaccard and binary = TRUE) in the R package vegan102,107. Afterward, we calculated mean pairwise dissimilarities for each site combination across all taxa. We then visualized the patterns in community composition using a non-metric multidimensional scaling (NMDS) analysis of the mean pairwise dissimilarities for each plot combination. We used the envfit function from the R package vegan102,107 to fit environmental vectors onto the ordination of dissimilarities. The resulting plot coordinates on the NMDS scale were grouped by land-use type. In addition, significant differences among land uses were tested using an analysis of similarities (ANOSIM) on the pairwise Jaccard dissimilarity matrix using the ANOSIM function (permutations = 9999) from the R package vegan102,107. To test whether land use had an effect at the ecosystem level, including biotic and abiotic variables, we ran a multiple factor analysis. This analysis enables the identification of a common structure across two or more data matrices without assuming causation44, with canonical ordination methods being among the most powerful approaches for testing ecological relationships in a multivariate context44. To quantify the overall similarity (matrix correlation) between taxonomic groups in the multiple factor analysis, we used the RV coefficient, where 0 indicates no similarity and 1 indicates perfect similarity (Supplementary Table 1). We implemented this additional metric to test the robustness of our conclusions.

A GDM model was applied to each taxonomic group. We used the respective species matrix, the selected principal components for each group of environmental variables (see the section ‘Environmental data’), and the geographic plot coordinates to run the model. The execution of the GDM was performed using the gdm R package108. The contributions of environmental variables (principal components; Extended Data Fig. 7) and distance were estimated by extracting the maximum spline values (Supplementary Table 3). Significance testing of variables was performed using Monte Carlo sampling, implemented in the gdm.varImp function, with 250 permutations (Supplementary Table 2). All the analyses were performed in R v4.5.1 (ref. 109).

Further information on research design is available in the Nature Portfolio Reporting Summary linked to this article.

Data for the statistical analyses and main figures are stored in a Figshare repository (https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.31784410 (ref. 110)). Recorded (morpho-)species across taxa for canopy and leaf litter arthropods, butterflies, mesostigmatid mites and oribatid mites are deposited in the Ecotaxonomy database (http://ecotaxonomy.org). For birds, the automated sound recordings were uploaded to ecoSound-web (https://ecosound-web.de/ecosound_web/). Aural detections were confirmed with cross-checks on the Xeno-Canto online bird call database (http://xeno-canto.org/). Fungi have been deposited in the Dryad repository (https://doi.org/10.5061/dryad.7h44j0zrd (ref. 82)).

Code for the statistical analyses and main figures are available in a Figshare repository (https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.31784410 (ref. 110)).

Venn diagrams include aboveground taxonomic groups together or each group separately. They illustrate the shared and unique species, along with their percentages, across land-use types (i.e., γ-diversity). Land-use types are: forest (F), jungle rubber (J), rubber plantation (R), and oil palm plantation (O).

Venn diagrams include aboveground taxonomic groups together or each group separately. They illustrate the shared and unique species numbers and percentages across land-use types (i.e., γ-diversity). Land-use types are: forest (F), jungle rubber (J), rubber plantation (R), and oil palm plantation (O).

Multidiversity across scales was calculated using standardized values (min-max scaling approach). For α-, and β-multidiversity, significant differences tested using two-sided ANOVA Type III. Linear model fits using ggeffect (marginal mean and confidence intervals, n = 32 plots). For γ-multidiversity aboveground, values shifted from 0.99, 0.72, 0.18, and 0.07 in forest, jungle rubber, rubber and oil palm plantations, while γ-multidiversity belowground, values shifted from 0.74, 0.73, 0.21, and 0.51 in forest, jungle rubber, rubber and oil palm plantations, respectively. For α-multidiversity aboveground, values shifted from 0.64 (95% CIs: 0.58 − 0.70), 0.47 (0.41 − 0.53), 0.24 (0.18 − 0.30), and 0.22 (0.16 − 0.28) in forest, jungle rubber, rubber, and oil palm plantations, while α-multidiversity belowground, values shifted from 0.50 (0.44− 0.56), 0.48 (0.42 − 0.54), 0.32 (0.26 − 0.38), and 0.41 (0.35 − 0.47) in forest, jungle rubber, rubber and oil palm plantations, respectively (n = 32 plots). For β-multidiversity aboveground, values varied from 0.42 (0.37 − 0.47), 0.52 (0.47−0.57), 0.54 (0.49−0.59), 0.49 (0.44− 0.54) in forest, jungle rubber, rubber and oil palm plantations, respectively, while β-multidiversity belowground, values were consistent across land uses ~0.45.

Pearson correlations calculated using stats and correlations plotted using ggscatter (mean and confidence intervals; n = 8 plots for land-use type).

Points and lines (mean and 95% confidence intervals using 10,000 bootstrap replicates) represent log ratio in diversity associated with land-use intensification using forests as a control. CIs not overlapping zero indicate differences from the forest (coloured points; black CIs; shaded when the 95% CIs include zero). Negative and positive values indicate decreases or increases in turnover or nestedness, respectively, relative to mean forest values.

Environmental groups include litter (cumulative percentage of variance = 86%), microclimate (cumulative percentage of variance = 90%), soil (cumulative percentage of variance = 84%), and vegetation (cumulative percentage of variance = 84%). Variables and abbreviations are explained in Supplementary Table 5. For each variable group, dimensions were selected until 80% of the explained variance was reached. Colour shades indicate the selected dimensions of the principal component analyses, with the darkest shades representing the first dimension and lighter shades representing higher dimensions (up to dimension four in the soil group).

Supplementary Results, Supplementary Figs. 1–10, Supplementary Tables 1–5 and Supplementary references.

Multiple comparisons using t-test to assess significant differences between the log ratio and zero (forests as a reference), adjusting the P values using the false discovery rate.

#1369. Ex-Napoli striker takes aim at Allegri over Hojlund with cryptic social media post

Former Napoli striker Roberto Sosa took a cryptic dig at Massimiliano Allegri, asking why Rasmus Hojlund keeps scoring for Denmark while struggling to match those numbers for Napoli.

Hojlund has just started his second season at Napoli, but has only managed three goals in 14 appearances across all competitions under new coach Allegri.

His numbers with the Danish national team are very different, as the former Manchester United striker has netted six goals in his last six international appearances.

Sosa, a former Napoli striker, seems convinced that Hojlund’s poor form is tied to Allegri’s tactics.

“After dinner, after a nice digestif, don’t the coach’s friends ever ask themselves why the striker always scores for his national team but doesn’t score nearly as many goals (at least so far) for his club? Enjoy your meal,” Sosa wrote on X.

Sosa’s posts drew mixed reactions from Napoli fans, with some urging him to be less critical of the team and others backing his views.

Therefore, the former Argentine striker shared another post, this time a video from the seaside.

“After you’ve watched this video, you are free to write to me: ‘Pampa, I’m going to block you.’ And I’ll react with a heart,” he said.

“I watch every Napoli game, every Serie A, Premier League and European competition. If a team plays badly, I can’t say otherwise; I have to examine ball possession, counter-pressing, how they track back, and how they try to win those games. Then, I might note injuries, whether certain teams didn’t buy any players. But to me, we shouldn’t start backward, as some do, creating excuses or alibis. Well, those are the famous like-chasers. I wish you a good day, a good lunch and a good dinner!”

#1368. Thomas Tuchel is now embracing traditional English values - clarity has helped England understand who they are, and now they can beat the best, writes CRAIG HOPE

Published: 16:57 EST, 16 November 2026 | Updated: 16:57 EST, 16 November 2026

Thomas Tuchel has always liked what he sees from his England players on the training pitch. Less so, at times, inside a stadium. It is a contradiction with which he has wrestled since the World Cup, when performances on the whole left him underwhelmed, save for the collective spirit and individual excellence that rescued results.

It is why, when the squad reconvened at St George’s Park in September, Tuchel used the meeting room as much as he did the grass to address that disparity in delivery.

At the same time, the elephant in the corner of the auditorium was the German’s own comments about the DNA of English players compared to the likes of Spain, and fundamentally them lacking the coding to protect possession and, therefore, valuable leads. He asked Harry Kane, Jude Bellingham and others for their thoughts.

The message back from his players was this – let us be better at being us, not them. Interestingly, that was Tuchel’s mantra upon his appointment, one of embracing traditional English values. Amid the World Cup fallout, though, he had wandered in a daze down a rabbit hole of genetics, focusing on what his team cannot do as opposed to what they can.

Tuchel, his staff and his players are tacticians and technicians, not scientists. If the intricacies of DNA do not allow them to be Spain, then don’t be. Be England, they determined. That is not to say kick and rush, bark and bite. After all, Kane is officially the best player in the world right now and Bellingham, unofficially, is playing as well as anyone on the planet.

Rather, there needed to be clarity – this is what we are and this is how we beat the best. On Sunday night in Madrid, England beat the very best. It was a victory born from those hours on the training field and in conference, and even more spent by Tuchel and his assistant Anthony Barry during their post-tournament review in a St George’s Park war room. They knew then that this was not a case of rip it up and start again, more so mend the tears and give the likes of Bellingham a blank sheet to impact where, and how, he sees best.

Thomas Tuchel is embracing England's DNA and reaping the rewards following the World Cup

England can now beat the best, which they showed against Spain in a fantastic victory

There was no radical strategical change, but there was a new doctrine, principles that should underpin whatever the in-game circumstance – off-the-ball running, a high press, filling in for a team-mate who has seized a moment to improvise elsewhere, such as the full backs. Ben White scoring England’s third on Sunday and Lewis Hall completing four more dribbles than Lamine Yamal were examples of Tuchel’s allowance for greater intuition. Be you, not Spain.

Kane, informally at least, has also been promoted beyond captain, a bridge between management and dressing-room. To see him in a semi-coaching and cajoling capacity on the touchline after he was taken off in the 78th minute against Spain was to witness this elevation.

But even if England had conceded a late equaliser at the Metropolitano Stadium, it would not have mattered. Not when it comes to measuring post World Cup improvement. To have drawn comparison with Argentina and that second-half collapse would have been unfair and inaccurate. The semi-final was 11 versus 11 and so let us judge this game on the same terms. And what did England do with a 1-0 lead and 11 players? They attacked. And attacked again. For all of the tweaks Tuchel and Barry have made to the structure of training and the team’s set-up, this was evidence of them learning from a mistake, as much as the head coach will be loath to admit.

Ezri Konsa, however, did reveal there was a definite instruction to keep attacking Spain when Tuchel addressed the team at half-time.

‘The instruction was to keep going at them,’ said the defender. ‘Don’t stop. To keep our foot on the pedal. That is what we did. Argentina was different, different circumstances. But it was not just half-time. We went 1-0 up and Harry, our captain, told us to keep going and to keep our foot on the pedal too.'

Before Jarell Quansah’s needless mistake and Elliot Anderson’s subsequent dismissal in the 63rd minute, the game was not in the balance in any way. As a live observer of almost every Tuchel match since his arrival, this was the best performance of his reign. In fact, it’s not even close.

And yet, so much still comes back to Bellingham. England would not have won without him. He terrified Spain, perhaps given their intimate knowledge of his powers. Beating the best is as much a mental challenge as it is physical, and Bellingham believed. He made England believe, too. His swagger. His majesty. And yes, his skill. He won the corner for Konsa’s headed second and created the third for White. He then dropped into midfield when down to ten and battled and organised like a captain.

Bellingham has bought into the collective under Tuchel and, with that, his team-mates are buying into his big ideas. For now, they don’t come much bigger than what England achieved in Madrid.

#1367. Raimondo: Frosinone stars reveals where he must improve to earn Italy call-up

Frosinone striker Antonio Raimondo says he must improve in two areas before earning a senior Italy call-up and names Euro 2020 winner Ciro Immobile as one of his role models.

Raimondo is one of Serie A’s top scorers this season, with eight goals in ten league games. The 22-year-old hasn’t yet received an Italy call-up and, perhaps, only a recent injury has kept him out of Roberto Mancini’s squad for the November break.

“I’m not thinking about expectations placed on me. When things go well, you are always good; when they don’t, you become the worst. I think it’s important to find balance,” Raimondo told Tuttosport.

When asked about his role models, the Frosinone star replied: “Cavani, Icardi and Immobile. Three fantastic strikers, and I’d like to take something from all of them. I still watch games of great players to study their movements and understand their mindset: being clinical in front of goal, how to attack space, or move into open field.”

Raimondo already discussed a potential Italy call-up in previous interviews, so what does he need to do to finally fulfil his dream?

“I must keep doing what I’m doing – he replied – and try to improve in the areas I mentioned before: playing with my shoulders to the goal and linking up with my teammates.”

Frosinone are arguably the biggest surprise in Serie A this season, as the newly promoted side sits 6th in the standings, ahead of Juventus and Napoli. Can they aim for something more than survival?

“First, we think about survival, and once we’ve achieved that, we’ll think about something different,” Raimondo concluded.

#1365. Conte vs. Spalletti: The financial gap behind Napoli’s success

Both Antonio Conte and Luciano Spalletti delivered a Scudetto to Napoli, yet the club’s spending and operating costs rose dramatically under the Lecce-born tactician.

La Gazzetta dello Sport has compared Napoli’s transfer spending over the last four seasons: two under Spalletti and two under Conte.

The Partenopei invested €367m during the Conte era: €152m in the 2024-25 season and another €215m in 2025-26. Player sales only partially offset those figures, generating €223m overall and leaving the club with a net transfer deficit of €144m.

The heavy transfer spending left its mark on the club’s finances. Wage costs rose to €142m in 2024-25 and €172m in 2025-26, with amortisation expenses going from €111m to €128m.

As a result, the combined cost of wages and amortisation reached €253m in 2024-25 and climbed to €300m in 2025-26. In practical terms, these costs absorbed 87% and 78% of Napoli’s revenue in Conte’s two seasons.

Luciano Spalletti’s era, which brought the first Scudetto since Diego Armando Maradona, was built on a more restrained financial model. During the Tuscan’s two-year spell, the transfer spending totalled €109m, while player sales generated €91m.

Combined wage and amortisation costs never exceeded €200m during the Spalletti era.

The gap is evident in performance as well. Although both coaches won one Serie A title, each Serie A point in the Spalletti era cost Napoli €2.3m compared to €3.5m under Conte.

Napoli’s biggest stars during the Spalletti era, Khvicha Kvaratskhelia and Victor Osimhen, were sold when Conte was in charge for €80m and €75m, respectively. Kvara played only six months under Conte, while Osimhen never featured under the Lecce-born coach, but their sales proved crucial in financing transfers over the last two seasons.

Lorenzo Bettoni is the Editor of Football Italia.

#1364. Man Utd make worst start in 40 years after being hauled back by 10-man Spurs

Manchester United fans were never going to pass up the opportunity to aim a volley of abuse in the direction of their bitter rivals.

By the end of another deeply unconvincing performance, though, they were more preoccupied by the problems afflicting their own team than the cheating scandal engulfing Manchester City.

Against City at Old Trafford last month, United lost to a team who were down to 10 men after just 23 minutes.

This time around they could not hold on to a lead against a Tottenham Hotspur side also navigating a numerical disadvantage following Rodrigo Bentancur’s sending off.

Rodrigo Bentancur dives in on Luke Shaw and it's all kicking off at Old Trafford! 🫨 https://t.co/uJUAMuZNzc

The sum total of it all is that United have now made their worst start to a season for 40 years, which is saying something given the traumas of the post-Ferguson era, and perhaps more disconcertingly, look to all intents and purposes like a team going backwards.

The bounce they enjoyed under Michael Carrick last season en route to Champions League qualification is over and, after just six points from as many games, it is hard to shake the feeling that it is going to be anything but a serious battle to finish in the top four or five.

The supporters did not hide their disgruntlement. There were boos around the half hour mark after an insipid opening when Spurs did everything but score and a slow, sluggish, dishevelled United almost looked impervious to their troubles.

Carrick had called for his players to show some “fire” coming into this match, but instead watched them ambling around like it was all a terrible inconvenience. The ease with which Spurs ran around them was alarming. There were more jeers at the interval and again at full time.

Carrick admitted that “hurt” although not as much you suspect as the sight of players feigning interest and then throwing away three points when they had finally summoned some fight to lead courtesy of Bryan Mbeumo’s goal.

Bryan Mbeumo slots it home to give Manchester United the lead against Spurs! 🎯 https://t.co/7yKnpyhfUe

It was a lovely finish after good work by the largely anonymous Matheus Cunha, and when Bentancur was sent off five minutes later after butting Luke Shaw, it should have been the cue to see out the game. To fail to do so against a side as toothless as Tottenham made it all the worse. Leading late on against Everton last month, they also failed to get over the line. It cannot keep happening.

Equally, United cannot play like they did in the first half here when they face Atlético Madrid in the Spanish capital on Tuesday night or at Elland Road against bitter rivals Leeds five days later and expect to get anything from either game. They are not the sort of matches Carrick would want with his team in this shape, but they need to find some inspiration from somewhere.

Carlos Baleba coming on around the hour mark and making a difference on his debut will at least offer Carrick some grounds for encouragement. The £65m midfield signing from Brighton offers some energy and urgency and looks a more natural bedfellow for Kobbie Mainoo than Youri Tielemans, who was woeful against Spurs and should have come off earlier.

In truth, Tielemans was not alone. Throughout the team there was a disconnect and unease and Carrick admitted it became contagious.

“We just couldn’t find a way to get ourselves into the game, whether that was with the ball or without the ball,” the United manager said. “We were a little bit slow with the decision-making, didn’t quite see the passing areas, the space. You don’t want it to happen, but sometimes it can and it probably spread through the team a little bit too much.”

It does not help that Bruno Fernandes is being hampered by an injury he has been carrying for weeks or that Carrick has no natural centre-forward to call upon with Benjamin Sesko again sidelined by the recurrence of a worrying shin problem. Amad Diallo did return here after a lengthy lay-off of his own, but did not look match fit.

In defence, Lisandro Martínez did enough to put off Dominic Solanke, who fired over from Sávio’s cross in the second half, but this was otherwise another poor showing from the Argentine centre-back, one of several positions where United need upgrades.

United needed shaking badly, but when Carrick turned to his bench he called upon Joshua Zirkzee, a fitful forward the club wanted to sell this summer, and right-back Diogo Dalot in addition to Baleba.

Marcus Rashford cannot have been fit given he was only introduced in the 95th minute and perhaps the same was true of the unused Mason Mount. As for £50m summer signing Andrey Santos, this was another league game when the Brazilian midfielder did not get a look in.

United fans had taunted Spurs when a goal and a man up. “You’re going down with the City,” they crowed, a nod to the possibility of City being expelled or relegated from the Premier League after being found guilty of breaching more than 100 financial rules.

United fans had also revived their Stretford End “ticker” after reaching the conclusion that none of City’s titles under Abu Dhabi ownership had been won fairly so, in their eyes, it is now 50 years since their rivals last won anything legitimately. City, of course, continue to maintain their innocence and have lodged an appeal.

But United fans were unable to crow for too long once Solanke levelled.

Spurs are level in stoppage-time! 😳 https://t.co/NoivNchgWw

It had been similar early in the game when the home fans had trained their sights on City. “You cheating b--------, you know what you are”, they sang lustily.

But as the match wore on, those chants began to quieten as the crowd, taking their lead from the team, fell decidedly flat.

Carrick is going to have to find a spark from somewhere and quickly.

Speaking to BBC Match of the Day, Carrick said: “It was a mixed game. We found it tough to start with. For a number of reasons, we were not quite there. You could see it was a challenging time.

“But the lads grew into the game, in the second half I thought we were better in everything. To get the game as we wanted it, in such a good position - we should see it through. We have to manage those situations. That’s two late goals which have hurt us, and things look very different. That’s the reality.”

When asked about the boos at half-time and full-time, he replied: “It’s not nice, it hurts a lot because I care about this club. But I understand the disappointment, the reality is what it is, we need to get back to winning games.”

Spurs have been on top in this half but there has been a lack of quality from both teams. It has been a scrap between two average teams. Conor Gallagher the most influential player on the pitch so far.

Following Solanke and Kudus’ earlier chances, Spurs have been quiet going forward. Man Utd have been slowly growing into the game.

Amad is dribbling with intent and Gallagher bumps into him. The referee doesn’t give a free-kick and the home fans aren’t happy with that decision. It’s also worth remembering that Gallagher is on a yellow card. He needs to be careful.

Amad forces a save from Kinsky! Man Utd clear a Tottenham corner and burst forward on the counter through Mbeumo. The former Brentford man is chased by Tonali and has Amad in support, before playing the pass into the 24-year-old. Udogie closes down the angle, forcing Amad to take the chance with a first-time shot. His fizzing strike is comfortably collected by Kinsky, but that is more encouraging from the hosts.

You can feel the nervousness in the Old Trafford crowd. Spurs’ dominance has calmed over the last 10 minutes, but Man Utd have failed to take control or pick up the tempo.

This game looks it could be time for Baleba’s much-anticipated debut. Man Utd’s current midfield doesn’t possess enough running power and Tottenham are exploiting that.

Man Utd’s slow start prompts some boos from the home fans. Cunha attempts to rally the crowd, but his side have given their supporters nothing to be positive about in this game so far. From a Spurs perspective, you can see why they’ve only scored two top-flights goals this season. They should be two-nil up, but they’ve notably lacked end-product.

Tottenham miss another golden chance! It’s a brilliant passing move from defence to attack. It ends with Savio teeing up Kudus with an intelligent cross. The Ghanaian can’t quite fully wrap his foot around the delivery, and from inside the penalty area, he slams an unmarked effort wide of the bottom corner.

Currently, Man Utd are being outnumbered in midfield. The interchangeability of Tonali, Bergvall and Gallagher is running rings around Mainoo and Tielemans. Fernandes’ lack of defensive instinct is leaving the hosts’ midfield pivot exposed.

Man Utd then make a rare foray forward as Cunha whips in a cross towards Amad. Udogie is alert to the danger and gets in front of the winger to clear.

Ex-Nottingham Forest manager Steve Cooper is here in the directors’ box at Old Trafford. He was last at Brondby in Denmark and will inevitably be considered for jobs here in England as chairmen look to make changes during the season.

Still, it’s Tottenham forcing the issue as Kudus dashes past Shaw with his blistering pace. Cunha tracks back but can’t stop the winger from digging out a cross. Yoro’s skewed clearance is headed back to Lammens by Tielemans. Man Utd need to careful, they cannot continue playing like this.

The visitors then steam forward again on the counter. On this occasion, Yoro defends magnificently, executing a well-timed sliding tackle on Van Hecke.

The visitors have made an excellent start to this game. Savio breezes past Maguire like he isn’t even there, but can’t quite find Kudus with his low cross. De Zerbi will want his side to capitalise on this dominant period. Man Utd look sluggish and asleep so far.

Gallagher receives an early yellow card after pulling Maguire back. Referee Attwell isn’t taking any prisoners. Man Utd supporters also show their love and appreciation for Rui Pinto with this banner.

Tottenham waste a huge chance! What is Lammens doing?! The Man Utd goalkeeper tries to pick out Mainoo with a very risky pass. It’s intercepted by Bergvall, who tees up Solanke. One-on-one with Lammens, the Spurs striker’s whipped effort is blocked by Lammens. The Belgian goes from zero to hero, emphatically redeeming himself.

We are under way at Old Trafford. Can either of these sides pick up a victory to relieve the pressure on their head coach?

“You cheating b******s, you know what you are,” is heard from the stands at Old Trafford. It’s pretty safe to say they are referring to Manchester City’s guilty verdict which was announced during the international break.

Man Utd, skippered by Fernandes, receive a feverish reception as they’re welcomed onto the pitch by the Old Trafford faithful. Tottenham are led out by Solanke, who captains the visitors today.

With kick-off fast approaching, here’s a recap of both line-ups.

Man Utd: Lammens, Yoro, Maguire, Martinez, Shaw, Tielemans, Mainoo, Diallo, Fernandes, Mbeumo, Cunha.

Matheus Cunha, who has struggled in a false nine role, is likely to revert to the left with Marcus Rashford on the bench so I suspect Bryan Mbeumo will play through the middle with Amad off the right, and Bruno Fernandes in behind Mbeumo. Hello and welcome to our live coverage of this mouthwatering Premier League game between Manchester United and Tottenham at Old Trafford.

If Manchester City had not entered a legal battle with the Premier League after being found guilty of breaching 114 charges relating to financial regulations by an independent panel, then surely there would be more pressure on the two head coaches in the dugout this evening?

Man Utd and Tottenham have undoubtedly both endured extremely disappointing starts to their respective top-flight campaigns. The hosts sit just inside the bottom half of the table after picking up just five points from their opening five matches. It’s going even worse for Tottenham, who languish in 20th with zero wins and just two points.

The perilous landscape leaves only one reasonable conclusion: this has all the ingredients for an early season six-pointer.

The strain is perhaps less intense on Michael Carrick, with the Englishman having built up a bundle of goodwill after cleaning up the mess left by Ruben Amorim last season as Man Utd eventually finished third, qualifying for the Champions League. Fans were left slightly underwhelmed by the club’s transfer window, with the players at Carrick’s disposal having not forged any momentum so far in this campaign.

The spotlight is definitely shining more intensely upon Roberto De Zerbi after big-spending Tottenham splashed over £300m in the summer on the likes of Sandro Tonali, Mateus Fernandes, Jan Paul van Hecke and Savio. However, the Italian boss is yet to strike the correct rhythm with his newly-formed squad. An encouraging performance backed up by a positive result here at Old Trafford could be the perfect antidote to ease the worries of fans fearing that Tottenham could be embroiled in another relegation battle.

All eyes are on this one. Kick-off is at 17:30, with team news coming shortly.

#1363. Scotland skipper Andy Robertson insists time is running out for Pocognoli's men after horror show in St Gallen

By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER

Published: 17:35 EST, 16 November 2026 | Updated: 17:41 EST, 16 November 2026

Andy Robertson admitted Scotland don’t have time to get things right under Sebastien Pocognoli after the team were humbled by Switzerland on the night of the skipper’s record 103rd cap.

John McGinn warned this week it could take the Scots up to 18 months to fully grasp the Belgian’s tactical plans.

But serious questions are now being asked of Pocognoli after his team were swept aside in a miserable 4-0 defeat to a much-changed Swiss side.

The result, combined with Slovenia’s 3-0 win over North Macedonia, ended Scotland’s already scant hopes of a Nations League promotion play-off spot and condemned them to pot three in next month’s Euro 2028 draw.

Robertson was hoping for a night to remember as he overtook Kenny Dalglish as the country’s most capped player but was clearly furious as the Scots crumbled in St Gallen.

Asked if it was going to take time for things to click under Pocognoli, he told the BBC: ‘I don’t think you’ve got time in international football, you have to do it.

Scotland skipper Andy Robertson laments a night to forget on the occasion of his 103rd cap

‘These supporters who travel everywhere, are they going to give us time? No. Are the people inside Hampden going to give us time? No. Are the people outside Hampden, who are going to be critical and rightly so? No.

‘We don’t have time, the players do not have time, we have got to step up.

‘We have a long break now to March, which is not a good thing, and it is going to be a tough one to swallow.

‘We really need to step up again. In international football, you do not have time.’

After an unconvincing start to his reign, Pocognoli needed a statement victory to convince sceptical fans that he is the right man for the job.

Despite a promising start, the rot set in after Lewis Ferguson’s 22nd minute own-goal.

The Swiss, missing a host of key players, went further ahead with goals from Winsley Boteli, Alvyn Sanches and Zeki Amdouni.

Almost 12 months on from the famous night when Steve Clarke’s side beat Denmark to reach the World Cup, the Tartan Army will be looking towards the European qualifiers with trepidation.

Robertson is tackled by Switzerland's Zachary Athekame on a night of few positives

Robertson said: ‘First half, I thought we were in the game. We lost a stupid goal but I thought we had chances and it could have been 2-1 at half-time.

‘By the time you get to 50 minutes and you are 3-0 down, that can’t happen in international football.

‘We were playing a good team but I felt we were in the game, it is a really tough night for us.’

Pocognoli also felt the final scoreline was harsh and rued his side’s inability to make the most of the opportunities they created.

‘The score is heavy with the 4-0, but I don’t think it’s a reflection of the game, if I’m really honest and objective,’ said Pocognoli.

‘I think we had some very good moments, we started like we wanted, aggressive away from home. I think we played a good first half, we created chances, we were dominant in some moments and we faced Switzerland with different shapes and adapted well from the first minute.

Sebastien Pocognoli will now face some searching questions over his suitability for the job

‘I think we conceded the goal from maybe one of the first chances they had. We also created chances but we were not clinical in that moment in the box.

‘In the second half, yeah, we started poorly from the first minute, a poor corner we gave away. Then you feel that, OK, we will get punished.

‘But I think when we made the substitutions, they made an impact, and we should have scored two goals in that period.

‘At the end, it’s a bad feeling, the score, but I think that the players try to do their best and create moments that we want to see.’

#1362. Why Former Manchester United Star Wes Brown Was Declared Bankrupt

Nick is a combat sports writer and editor for GIVEMESPORT - with eight years of experience in the industry.

Nick started out with the GIVEMESPORT Academy in 2018 and has also previously worked as a combat sports editor for Sportskeeda. In his current role with the site, Nick produces and edits news pieces, features and evergreen articles on a wide variety of sports.

A fan of the sweet science since childhood, Nick has attended over 100 boxing and UFC events including Manny Pacquiao vs Ricky Hatton, Floyd Mayweather vs Miguel Cotto, Deontay Wilder vs Tyson Fury II, Anthony Joshua vs Oleksandr Usyk and Canelo vs Crawford.

When not writing about boxing or MMA, Nick can be found watching cricket, rugby and darts, as well as cheering on Leeds United at Elland Road.

Former Manchester United defender and Champions League winner Wes Brown was declared bankrupt in May 2023 and ended up renting a property from an Old Trafford star. Brown spent a total of 19 years at the Theatre of Dreams, making 262 appearances and winning 14 trophies during his time at the club.

At the peak of his career, Brown was believed to be earning around £50,000-a-week at United, hence why many observers were shocked to learn of his financial woes just five years after he retired from the game.

Among the best right-backs in England during his peak years, Brown earned 23 caps for the Three Lions and famously set up Cristiano Ronaldo's opening goal in the 2008 Champions League final against Chelsea.

According to a report from the Daily Mail, the petition to make the 46-year-old bankrupt came from two parties. One was HMRC – who Brown was said to owe a six-figure sum in unpaid taxes – while the other was a car finance company due only a few thousand pounds.

A source close to Brown summed up his money problems when speaking to the Mail, telling the newspaper: "It may seem like Wes was earning big money - to most people he was - but the trouble was he was also trying to keep up with the lifestyle of teammates earning five or six times more than he was."

Brown's finances took a major hit in 2022 when he officially split from his wife of 12 years, Real Housewives of Cheshire star Leanne Wassell. Divorce proceedings were estimated to have cost Brown a significant sum, but his money worries appear to have begun because of several poor property investments.

GIVEMESPORT Key Statistic: Wes Brown made 308 Premier League appearances with Manchester United and Sunderland.

"Most of his money disappeared in bad property deals," revealed the source. "He overpaid on the farm that Leanne lives in. He spent something like £6 million or £7 million to buy that.

The former Manchester United defender was declared bankrupt last year.

"They have tried to sell it but haven’t managed to, even after lowering the price to £4.75 million. Any money left is tied up in the farm. A previous property of theirs was once listed at £4.5 million but took seven years to sell, finally going for £2.4 million - almost half price."

Several of Brown's former United colleagues rallied around him after learning of his bankruptcy, according to the same report. Wayne Rooney and Michael Carrick offered their support, while Marcus Rashford went one step further in helping out as he is believed to be letting Brown stay in one of his lavish Manchester properties at what were described as 'mates rates'.

In 2024, Brown spoke out about his financial troubles and claimed he had the wrong people around him when earning his professional salary at Manchester United. He told the Ben Heath Podcast:

"I think the main thing is when you are making a lot of money, you need the right people, don't you? And I would say that's one of the things I didn't have."

Brown added: "It was a little bit different. It wasn't lots of people you go and speak to, and you maybe meet people and do this, do that. I wasn't interested in any of that. You said yes and got on with it.

A Liverpool icon is among the latest to file for bankruptcy after failing to manage his finances post-retirement.

"It's a long story and I won't go into detail, but it's stuff that happened a long time ago with certain investments and getting into stuff that, as a young kid, a lot of people go into, [but] don't really understand it. It's what a lot of people are doing and then it came to a head last year, and that's how it went.

"I think the main thing going forward for me is I'm very lucky to still be doing what I'm doing and getting on with it. It's not a nice thing, but I'm not the sort of person to cry about it or moan about it."

Brown has endured the highest of highs and the lowest of lows – and a pivotal aspect of him getting back to his professional best has been to continue working throughout. Speaking to Express Sport, he said: "Well, luckily, I still work, so that’s good.

"But it’s all been sorted now in the sense that I know what I need to do and everybody is happy with everything," the former defender said. "So I’m just getting on with it now and carrying on really."

It was a tough ride, it’s something that is hard to deal with on your own at times. But luckily I still do quite a lot of work and I'm able to carry on now moving forward. Today I’m one more day out of it.

As he continues to get to grips with post-retirement life, one of his active roles includes educating current athletes on the importance of financial literacy and due diligence. It's all in an attempt to issue guidance that was not available at the height of his fame, while he was on the books of the Old Trafford-based outfit.

Statistics courtesy of Transfermarkt. Correct as of 18-11-26.

#1361. How much Napoli would save by selling De Bruyne in January

Reports in Italy over the last few weeks indicate that Kevin De Bruyne could leave Napoli as early as January, which could provide the Partenopei with around €10m to reinvest if they do allow the Belgian superstar to leave midway through the season.

De Bruyne is into the final year of the two-year contract he signed with Napoli after leaving Manchester City at the end of the 2024-25 season. There is an option to extend that agreement by a further 12 months, until the end of the 2027-28 season, but this appears an unlikely scenario at this stage.

Reports earlier this week claimed that Dutch side PSV Eindhoven are interested in pursuing a deal for De Bruyne, potentially as early as January, and that they are willing to offer around €2m to Napoli for the 35-year-old, who will have less than six months remaining on his contract during the next transfer window.

Some outlets claim that Napoli will hold out for a larger transfer fee, while others, including the Corriere dello Sport, still claim that Napoli wish to keep hold of De Bruyne until the end of the season at least.

There have also been suggestions that De Bruyne is keen on the idea of a move to the Netherlands, as he and his family could move into the home they own in the Belgian province of Limburg, which borders the Netherlands.

According to the latest updates from La Gazzetta dello Sport, what is becoming clear is that De Bruyne would need to take a significant pay cut if he is to join PSV during the January transfer window.

The Pink Paper claims that De Bruyne earns a net salary of around €5m per season with Napoli, which costs the club around €10m per season gross. La Gazzetta dello Sport reports that PSV would not ‘seem able to afford’ these figures.

If Napoli do offload De Bruyne in January, though, they will save half a season’s worth of wages, around €5m gross, plus around €2.5m in bonuses that would no longer be valid, as well as a transfer fee of €2m or above, which could provide Napoli with around €10m to reinvest in January.

Peter Young is a Senior Reporter with Football Italia.

#1360. Transient contacts between filaments impart its elasticity to branched actin

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Cells dynamically assemble actin into branched networks to push on their environment during cell migration, endocytosis or the maintenance of cell–cell contact1. These networks are among the stiffest found in the cytoskeleton and can generate large pushing stresses against stationary obstacles2,3,4,5. When grown against a controlled opposing stress in an atomic force microscope6 or inside the cell7, branched networks alter their own architecture to adapt their compressional stiffness to their environment, but the underpinnings of their mechanics and adaptability are unclear. Here we show that their high density and low connectivity place them outside the scope of standard elastic network models for actin. We show that they are instead dominated by the proliferation of interfilament contacts under compression. This places branched actin in the same category as undercoordinated fibrous materials such as sheep’s wool. When the network is grown under force, filaments entangle as if knitted together and trap contacts in their structure. Trapped contacts have a similar role as crosslinkers in rigidifying the network and are thus key to its active adaptive mechanics.
